Online Correlated Exponential Clocks Thanks: The code of the numerical verification in this paper is provided at Online-Correlated-Exponential-Clocks.git.

Zhiyi Huang ††thanks: The University of Hong Kong. Email: zhiyi@cs.hku.hk.    Kalen Patton ††thanks: École polytechnique fédérale de Lausanne (EPFL). Email: kalen.patton@epfl.ch.    Peilin Yang ††thanks: The University of Hong Kong. Email: peilinyang@connect.hku.hk.    Jiahao Zhao ††thanks: The University of Hong Kong. Email: zjiahao@connect.hku.hk.
November 7, 2026

In online resource allocation, we seek to allocate an incoming sequence of requests j∈𝒥j\in\mathcal{J} among a set of offline resources i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}, where decisions must be made immediately without knowledge of the future. State-of-the-art results typically follow from relax-and-round methods. For many problems, recent advances have come from improved methods of online rounding with negative correlations. However, such rounding schemes have largely been implemented on a case-by-case basis, making it difficult to transfer improvements and new ideas between problem settings. This leads us to ask the question: Can we develop unified methods of online rounding with negative correlations which can obtain state-of-the-art guarantees across different resource allocation settings?

We answer this question affirmatively by introducing the framework of Online Correlated Exponential Clocks (OCEC). In this framework, fractional allocations xi​jx_{ij} are assigned exponential clocks Yi​j∼Exp⁡(xi​j)Y_{ij}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(x_{ij}), and each request jj is allocated to the resource ii with smallest Yi​jY_{ij}. The key idea is that the sequence (Yi​j)j(Y_{ij})_{j} for each fixed ii is negatively correlated via an OCEC generator, resulting in better-than-baseline guarantees.

Our contributions are two-fold: First, we introduce OCEC rounding as a problem-independent interface which any online algorithm can use. This isolates the challenge of online rounding into the self-contained problem of designing an effective OCEC generator. Second, we demonstrate the flexibility of this method by giving a single OCEC generator which yields improved competitive bounds in three distinct problems: 0.556 for Display Ads, 0.530 for AdWords, and 4.69 for squared-load balancing. Previous best results were obtained by Blanc and Charikar (FOCS 2021), Chen, Huang, and Sun (FOCS 2024), and Borst and Kashaev (SODA 2027), respectively.

1 Introduction

Online resource allocation has broad applications, such as assigning impressions to advertisers and jobs to machines. In these applications, the resources (e.g., advertisers or machines) are known in advance, while the requests (e.g., impressions or jobs) arrive over time. The arrival of a request reveals its values or processing sizes on the resources; the algorithm then assigns it immediately and irrevocably, without knowing future requests. The objective depends on the set of requests assigned to each resource. In matching [33], Display Ads [19], and AdWords [37], we seek to maximize the value of allocation, while in load balancing [1], we seek to minimize cost.

A common approach for such problems is to compute a fractional allocation for each arriving request and round it randomly. These fractional decisions are guided by online primal-dual analysis [5, 14], while the rounding scheme seeks to convert the fractional allocations into integral ones while minimizing additional loss incurred. The simplest choice, independent rounding, assigns each request according to its fractional allocation, independently of earlier decisions. This clearly preserves fractional allocations as marginal probabilities, but as it is forgetful of its rounding decisions, it may repeatedly overlook the same advertiser or overload the same machine.

By correlating rounding decisions, we can improve the objective while still preserving marginal probability. For example, suppose an advertiser pays one dollar if it receives at least one of two impressions, each assigned to it with probability 1/21/2. Independent rounding earns 7575 cents in expectation, whereas correlated rounding earns one dollar by giving the advertiser the second impression exactly when it misses the first. However, achieving such gains online is difficult. An advertiser that missed earlier impressions should be favored next, but two such advertisers may compete for the same impression. Moreover, the algorithm cannot plan the correlation in advance, since it does not see future requests.

Despite these difficulties, dependent rounding has driven much recent progress in online advertising and scheduling. In online advertising, Display Ads and AdWords admit (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-competitive algorithms under large-market assumptions [19, 37], whereas the optimal randomized competitive ratio for AdWords with general bids is strictly below 1−1/e1-1/e [39]. Without large-market assumptions, the greedy ratio of 1/21/2 remained the best known for both problems for over a decade. [18] introduced online correlated selection (OCS) to obtain the first ratio above 1/21/2 for Display Ads, and [26] adapted it to obtain the first such ratio for AdWords. Subsequent work improved the OCS guarantees and developed multiway and stochastic variants [42, 20, 4, 12, 16].11 1 See Section 1.3 for concurrent work [16] on Display Ads.

In scheduling, independent rounding is 55-competitive for online squared-load balancing [10], and [6] improved the ratio to 4.98434.9843 by implementing the correlated rounding of [28] online. That rounding scheme was developed for the offline minimization of total weighted completion time on unrelated machines. There, [9] first used negatively correlated rounding to break the long-standing 1.51.5-approximation barrier of independent rounding, and [28] and subsequent work [27, 8, 23, 34, 24] improved the approximation ratio further.

These online dependent rounding schemes are problem specific, and advances do not readily transfer. For example, multiway OCS improved Display Ads [4], but the first multiway OCS for AdWords came three years later [12].

1.1 Our Results

We introduce online correlated exponential clocks (OCEC) as a unified framework for online dependent rounding through exponential races. Each resource ii runs an independent OCEC generator, an online algorithm that takes the fractional allocation xi​jx_{ij} from each request jj as input and returns a clock Yi​jY_{ij}. For each request, the fractional allocations sum to one and are chosen independently of the rounding randomness. We impose two requirements on these clocks:

  1. 1.

    Each clock Yi​jY_{ij} follows the exponential distribution of rate xi​jx_{ij}.

  2. 2.

    The clocks Yi​jY_{ij} of different requests jj are negatively associated.

Each request jj goes to the resource with the smallest clock; we call this OCEC rounding. These requirements yield the following rounding guarantees, respectively:

  1. 1.

    Each resource wins with probability exactly its fractional allocation xi​jx_{ij}.

  2. 2.

    For a submodular reward or a supermodular cost of a resource’s assigned requests, it suffices to analyze that resource against fresh competing clocks [40].

A generator that draws fresh clocks yields independent rounding. By correlating a resource’s clocks across requests, a generator can reduce the chance of repeatedly overlooking it.

With this framework, we isolate a common pattern that has appeared both in earlier OCS [4] and in dependent rounding schemes for scheduling [28, 23, 24]. These works each build around a particular clock-generation mechanism,22 2 In OCEC terms, the iterative fair contention resolution of [28] can be recast as an exponential race once its Poisson tickets are read as arrival times; its online implementation by [6] then fits our definition of OCEC rounding. [23] and [24] explicitly use exponential races based on multivariate geometric and Dirichlet variables; the online Dirichlet construction likewise fits our definition. For request masses that are multiples of 1/m1/m, the multiway OCS of [4] can also be expressed in our framework. but this common underlying tool is somewhat obscured by their different problem-specific implementations. We formalize this tool for the first time in the abstract, providing an interface that any online algorithm can implement. This also separates OCEC design into a standalone problem. Different applications can then reuse an OCEC generator while tailoring the fractional allocation and analysis to their objectives.

Our second contribution is an OCEC generator that simultaneously improves the competitive ratios of three online problems. This generator runs a Poisson process of rate λ\lambda on an internal timeline and assigns each request jj the next interval IjI_{j} of length xi​jx_{ij}. The first age of IjI_{j} is the time between its first Poisson arrival and the preceding Poisson arrival, or zero if IjI_{j} contains no arrival. The generator returns a clock coupled with the first age of IjI_{j} through their distribution functions, so that larger first ages give smaller clocks and thus higher winning probabilities. Intuitively, a large first age for one request requires a long preceding gap without arrivals. Requests whose intervals lie within that gap have first age zero, so the coupling favors the request at the end of the gap while disfavoring those inside it. All three improvements, for Display Ads, AdWords, and squared-load balancing, use this single generator with the same arrival rate λ=4.5\lambda=4.5.33 3 This λ\lambda is approximately optimal for each of the three applications under our analyses. The applications differ in their fractional allocation rules and in when they use correlated rather than independent clocks.

1.2 Overview of Techniques

Here we discuss our main techniques and their relationship to the work of [4] and [6].

Negative association

The first crucial step in our analysis is the requirement that the clocks in our OCEC generators be negatively associated. This property lets us reduce the complex dynamics of multiple competing generators to an analysis of each generator in isolation. By the submodular dominance property of negatively associated random variables [40], replacing a resource’s competitors with fresh, independent clocks can only decrease its expected submodular reward (or for load balancing, increase its expected supermodular cost). Hence, we can analyze a “fresh-competitor process” for each resource separately, obtaining a lower bound on reward for the advertising problems and an upper bound on cost for squared-load balancing.

State tracking with age-measures

For our advertising problems, we track each generator’s state in the fresh-competitor process using an age-measure. Recall that the age is the time elapsed since the generator’s last Poisson arrival. For example, in matching, the measure records both the probability that a resource is still unmatched and the distribution of its age in those outcomes. These measures evolve predictably as requests arrive. This extra information matters because a longer wait since the last arrival makes the resource more likely to win when the next Poisson arrival occurs. For Display Ads and AdWords, we extend this state tracking to account for impression values and remaining budgets, respectively.

Primal-dual analysis via a potential function

We use a potential function on these age-measures to turn this state information into an online allocation rule and a competitive guarantee. Intuitively, the potential assigns a value to a resource’s remaining opportunities for reward. Each resource makes an offer for an arriving request based on this potential and the request’s value, and we allocate the request fractionally to the resources with the highest current offers. The potential also supplies the accounting for our primal-dual analysis: spent potential contributes to the resource’s dual variable, while the offers determine the request’s dual variable. We choose the potential so that the reward credited to each request pays for both contributions. Together with the allocation rule, this yields a bound comparing our expected reward to the offline optimum.

Relation with [4].

Our OCEC generator is inspired by the continuous limit of the multiway OCS of [4], in which their geometric arrival process becomes a Poisson process. Viewed through OCEC, their construction first converts arrival ages into desired winning probabilities, then couples these probabilities to exponential clocks. Ensuring that the clocks achieve the desired winning probabilities imposes an additional feasibility condition. Our generator maps the first arrival age directly to an exponential clock, avoiding this intermediate step and its associated restriction.

For Display Ads, we also retain more information across gaps, in which low-value requests interrupt the rounding guarantee at a higher level. Such low-value requests cannot earn a reward at that level, but they can affect future winning chances by disrupting the constructed negative correlations. The gap analysis of [4] simply discards correlation between requests before and after a gap. On the other hand, tracking the age-measure through the gap lets us account for some of the surviving correlation, limiting the resulting loss in our potential bound.

Covariance savings for load balancing.

For squared-load balancing, negative correlation reduces the probability of assigning two jobs to the same machine. Let Xi​jX_{ij} indicate whether job jj is assigned to machine ii, and let Ii​jI_{ij} be job jj’s interval on machine ii’s timeline. For two jobs j<kj<k that machine ii rounds with the OCEC generator (λ=4.5\lambda=4.5), we prove the covariance bound

Cov(Xi​j,Xi​k)≤−∫Ii​j∫Ii​kδ(v−u)dvdu,δ(d)=0.86exp(−d−253d2).\operatorname{Cov}(X_{ij},X_{ik})\leq-\int_{I_{ij}}\int_{I_{ik}}\delta(v-u)\,dv\,du,\qquad\delta(d)=0.86\exp\!\left(-d-\frac{25}{3}d^{2}\right).

Thus every pair of such jobs contributes a saving, which decays with their separation on the timeline.

Relation with [6].

Both [6] and this paper follow the online primal-dual framework, with some implementation differences.44 4 Both algorithms apply online dependent rounding only to small fractional allocations. [6] explicitly require the job size to be comparable to a dual variable tracking the machine’s expected load. We instead invoke OCEC rounding when independent rounding fails the local primal-dual inequality, which implies analogous size bounds. Our improved competitive ratio comes mainly from our covariance-saving bound. They partition jobs on each machine into groups of total fractional allocation at most one. For two jobs with infinitesimal fractional allocations, their guaranteed covariance-saving rate is 1−2/(e+1)≈0.4621-2/(e+1)\approx 0.462 within a group and zero across groups. Our bound has δ⁡(0)=0.86\delta(0)=0.86 and decays with distance, while remaining positive at every finite separation.

1.3 Further Related Work

Online matching.

[33] introduced online bipartite matching and gave the optimal (1−1/e)(1-1/e)-competitive Ranking algorithm for unweighted graphs under adversarial arrivals. [2] extended this guarantee to vertex-weighted matching by randomly perturbing vertex weights. The Display Ads [19] and AdWords [37] problems considered in this paper also generalize online matching. For further background and references, see the surveys [36, 25].

Online rounding for matching.

Besides the OCS literature, a related line of work studies online rounding of fractional bipartite matchings with vertexwise guarantees: each offline vertex ii is matched with probability at least a ρ\rho fraction of its total fractional allocation. This line overlaps with OCS as the algorithm of [20] provides such guarantees. However, improving the rounding ratio does not automatically yield an improved competitive ratio for online matching. [7] identified structured fractional matchings that admit lossless online rounding. [38] consider the stronger requirement of retaining a ρ\rho fraction of every edge’s marginal, which implies the vertexwise guarantee. They achieve ρ=0.652\rho=0.652, which [24] improve to 0.680.68.

Online load balancing.

[1] studied online load balancing under ℓp\ell_{p} norms, giving O⁡(p)O(p)-competitive algorithms for finite pp and showing that greedy is (3+2​2)(3+2\sqrt{2})-competitive for the sum of squared loads. [10] proved that this ratio is optimal for deterministic algorithms and gave a 55-competitive randomized algorithm based on independent rounding. [6] later showed that 55 is optimal among independent-rounding algorithms. [21] developed convex-duality analyses for load balancing with power costs and linear assignment costs, connecting these problems to online speed scaling. More recent work extends online load balancing to symmetric norms [31, 32] and develops integral online algorithms for broader classes of convex objectives [30].

Offline dependent rounding.

[43, 22] study offline dependent rounding that preserves marginals with negative correlation under cardinality and bipartite degree constraints, respectively. [3] introduced pipage rounding, which [11] extended to matroid constraints for monotone submodular maximization. Swap rounding [13] provides analogous marginal and correlation guarantees under matroid constraints, with concentration bounds for linear functions and lower-tail bounds for monotone submodular functions. These methods have access to the full fractional solution, whereas our framework must round each request upon arrival.

Concurrent Work on Display Ads.

In parallel with this work, [16] obtained a 0.5561950.556195-competitive algorithm for Display Ads, compared with our guarantee of 0.5562970.556297 (calculated in Section B.2). Both primal-dual analyses use a similar idea of tracking an age measure at each weight threshold. Their work follows the multiway OCS framework of [4], in which they map discrete ages to target winning probabilities for a tournament among sampled candidates. On the other hand, our generator uses continuous ages, which are mapped directly to exponential clocks.

For example, mutually independent random variables are negatively associated, and so are random indicators that sum to at most one [44].

3 Online Correlated Exponential Clocks

In this section, we formally define OCEC generators, rounding, and the “First-Age Poisson generator” that we will use across all our applications.

3.1 Definitions and Properties

Let ℐ\mathcal{I} be a finite set of offline resources (e.g., advertisers or machines) and 𝒥\mathcal{J} a finite set of online requests (e.g., impressions or jobs), with 𝒥\mathcal{J} indexed in arrival order. Throughout, Exp⁡(0)\mathrm{Exp}(0) is a point mass at ∞\infty and Exp⁡(∞)\mathrm{Exp}(\infty) is a point mass at 00 by convention.

2OCEC Generator.

An OCEC generator 𝒢\mathcal{G} is an online algorithm. It receives as input a sequence of fractional allocations x∈[0,1]𝒥x\in[0,1]^{\mathcal{J}}, one for each request, fixed independently of the algorithm’s internal randomness. Upon receiving each allocation xjx_{j}, it returns a clock Yj∈ℝ+∪{∞}Y_{j}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}\cup\{\infty\}. For every such input sequence, we require the following properties:

  1. 1.

    Exponential marginals:  For every j∈𝒥j\in\mathcal{J}, Yj∼Exp⁡(xj)Y_{j}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(x_{j}).

  2. 2.

    Negative association:  Clocks (Yj)j∈𝒥(Y_{j})_{j\in\mathcal{J}} are negatively associated.

3OCEC Rounding.

Given an OCEC generator 𝒢\mathcal{G} and fractional allocations x∈[0,1]ℐ×𝒥x\in[0,1]^{\mathcal{I}\times\mathcal{J}} satisfying ∑i∈ℐxi​j≤1\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}x_{ij}\leq 1 for every j∈𝒥j\in\mathcal{J}, fixed independently of the generators’ randomness, the corresponding OCEC rounding is as follows.

  1. 1.

    For each resource i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}, run an independent copy 𝒢i\mathcal{G}_{i} of 𝒢\mathcal{G}.

  2. 2.

    For each request j∈𝒥j\in\mathcal{J} and its fractional allocation (xi​j)i∈ℐ(x_{ij})_{i\in\mathcal{I}}:

    1. (a)

      Send xi​jx_{ij} to the generator 𝒢i\mathcal{G}_{i} for each ii, and let Yi​jY_{ij} be the returned clock.

    2. (b)

      Draw a fresh discard clock Y¯j∼Exp⁡(1−∑ixi​j)\bar{Y}_{j}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1-\sum_{i}x_{ij}).

    3. (c)

      Allocate jj to the resource with the minimum exponential clock Yi​jY_{ij}, if it is below Y¯j\bar{Y}_{j}.

Let SiS_{i} be the set of requests allocated to resource ii.

Since the clocks Yi​j∼Exp⁡(xi​j)Y_{ij}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(x_{ij}) and the discard clocks Y¯j∼Exp⁡(1−∑ixi​j)\bar{Y}_{j}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1-\sum_{i}x_{ij}) are independent across resources, and their total rate is 1, each ii has the smallest clock with probability xi​jx_{ij}. That is, OCEC rounding preserves the marginals.

5.

For any i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I} and any j∈𝒥j\in\mathcal{J}, 𝐏𝐫[j∈Si]=xi​j\mathbf{Pr}\bigl[j\in S_{i}\bigr]=x_{ij}.

The next lemma localizes the analysis of each resource ii to its own generator. Replacing the clocks of ii’s competitors with fresh ones cannot increase the expectation of any submodular function of SiS_{i}, nor decrease that of any supermodular one.

6.

Fix any i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I}, and let SiInd={j∈𝒥:Yi​j<Zj}S_{i}^{\mathrm{Ind}}=\{j\in\mathcal{J}:Y_{ij}<Z_{j}\} for fresh competing clocks Zj∼Exp⁡(1−xi​j)Z_{j}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1-x_{ij}). Then, for every submodular function f:2𝒥→ℝf:2^{\mathcal{J}}\to\mathbb{R},

𝐄⁡[f⁡(Si)]≥𝐄⁡[f⁡(SiInd)],\mathbf{E}\bigl[f(S_{i})\bigr]\geq\mathbf{E}\bigl[f(S_{i}^{\mathrm{Ind}})\bigr],

For each jj, the indicator of j∈Sij\in S_{i}, i.e., of mini′≠i⁡Yi′​j>Yi​j\min_{i^{\prime}\neq i}Y_{i^{\prime}j}>Y_{ij} and Y¯j>Yi​j\bar{Y}_{j}>Y_{ij}, is nondecreasing in the block (Yi′​j)i′≠i(Y_{i^{\prime}j})_{i^{\prime}\neq i} and Y¯j\bar{Y}_{j}, and these blocks are disjoint across jj. Lemma 4 then gives the conditional inequality for submodular ff; applying it to −f-f gives the supermodular case. ∎

3.2 First-Age Poisson Generator

We now describe an OCEC generator driven by a stationary Poisson process of rate λ\lambda on ℝ\mathbb{R}, with arrivals (Tk)k∈ℤ(T_{k})_{k\in\mathbb{Z}} indexed in increasing order so that T0≤0<T1T_{0}\leq 0<T_{1}. The age at time tt is A⁡(t)=t−max⁡{Tk:Tk≤t}A(t)=t-\max\{T_{k}:T_{k}\leq t\}, the time elapsed since the most recent arrival no later than tt. The age of an arrival TkT_{k} is Tk−Tk−1T_{k}-T_{k-1}, i.e., the age at the moment right before TkT_{k}. For a bounded interval II, let A^​(I)\widehat{A}(I) denote the first age of II, i.e., the age of the first arrival in II, or 00 if II contains no arrivals. Let FxF_{x} denote the cumulative distribution function of A^​(I)\widehat{A}(I) for an interval II of length xx; by stationarity, this distribution depends only on xx. A direct calculation, deferred to Appendix A, gives the following closed form.

7.

For every x>0x>0 and a≥0a\geq 0:

Fx​(a)={1+e−λ​x−(1+λ​a)​e−λ​a,0≤a<x;1−λ​x​e−λ​a,x≤a.F_{x}(a)=\begin{cases}1+e^{-\lambda x}-(1+\lambda a)e^{-\lambda a},&0\leq a<x;\\[2.15277pt] 1-\lambda xe^{-\lambda a},&x\leq a.\end{cases} (2)

The First-Age Poisson generator lays the incoming allocations consecutively on the timeline [0,∞)[0,\infty): each xjx_{j} receives the next interval IjI_{j} of length xjx_{j}. It transforms each A^​(Ij)\widehat{A}(I_{j}) into an exponential clock by a probability integral transform with FxjF_{x_{j}}, randomized when IjI_{j} contains no arrivals. The generator samples −T0-T_{0} and T1T_{1} independently from Exp⁡(λ)\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda) and generates subsequent arrivals online by successively adding independent Exp⁡(λ)\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda) gaps.

Note that Uj∼Unif⁡[0,1]U_{j}\sim\mathrm{Unif}[0,1] by construction, hence Yj∼Exp⁡(xj)Y_{j}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(x_{j}). Each clock is also nonincreasing in the first age of its interval, so the clocks are negatively associated if the first ages are. Intuitively, the first ages are negatively associated because a large first age in one interval requires a long empty stretch before its first arrival, which leaves less room for large first ages in the other intervals.

8.

For any pairwise disjoint intervals I1,…,InI_{1},\ldots,I_{n} of finite positive length, the first ages A^​(I1),…,A^​(In)\widehat{A}(I_{1}),\ldots,\widehat{A}(I_{n}) are negatively associated.

Proof.

We discretize time into cells [ℓ​δ,(ℓ+1)​δ)[\ell\delta,(\ell+1)\delta), ℓ∈ℤ\ell\in\mathbb{Z}, whose occupancies by Poisson arrivals are independent. The priority PℓP_{\ell} of an occupied cell ℓ\ell is one plus the number of consecutive empty cells before it; empty cells have priority 00. For small δ\delta, the first age of an interval is approximately δ\delta times the priority of its first occupied cell. Since the BKR inequality (Lemma 2) applies to finitely many independent variables, we first cap the priorities and consider min⁡{Pℓ,p¯}\min\{P_{\ell},\bar{p}\} for a positive integer p¯\bar{p}, so that each depends on finitely many cells.

We show that the capped priorities are negatively associated. Let EE and FF be upward-closed events determined by finite disjoint sets of capped priorities. A capped priority of at least p≥1p\geq 1 is certified by its occupied cell together with the p−1p-1 empty cells before it, and these certificates are disjoint across occupied cells, since no occupied cell lies among the empty cells preceding another. Since EE and FF are upward closed, these certificates show that whenever EE and FF both occur, they occur on disjoint sets of cells. The BKR inequality (Lemma 2) then gives

𝐏𝐫⁡[E∩F]=𝐏𝐫⁡[E□F]≤𝐏𝐫⁡[E]​𝐏𝐫​[F],\mathbf{Pr}[E\cap F]=\mathbf{Pr}[E\mathbin{\Box}F]\leq\mathbf{Pr}[E]\,\mathbf{Pr}[F],

which characterizes negative association (Lemma 1).

As the cap grows, the capped priorities converge to the priorities, which are therefore negatively associated by the closure under limits (Lemma 3). For each jj, let KjK_{j} be the set of cells contained in IjI_{j}, nonempty for small δ\delta, and let ℓj=min⁡Kj\ell_{j}=\min K_{j}. The discretized first age, δ\delta times the priority of the first occupied cell in KjK_{j}, or 00 if there is none, can be expressed as

A^δ(Ij)=δ∑ℓ∈KjPℓ 1{Pℓ≥ℓ−ℓj+1},\widehat{A}_{\delta}(I_{j})=\delta\sum_{\ell\in K_{j}}P_{\ell}\,\mathds{1}\{P_{\ell}\geq\ell-\ell_{j}+1\},

since Pℓ≥ℓ−ℓj+1P_{\ell}\geq\ell-\ell_{j}+1 exactly when ℓ\ell is the first occupied cell in KjK_{j}. This expression is nondecreasing in the priorities of the cells in KjK_{j}, and the sets KjK_{j} are disjoint across jj, so the discretized first ages are negatively associated by the closure under concordant monotone maps. Finally, A^δ​(Ij)→A^​(Ij)\widehat{A}_{\delta}(I_{j})\to\widehat{A}(I_{j}) almost surely as δ→0\delta\to 0, and the closure under limits completes the proof. ∎

In fact, the proof shows that, for every δ\delta, any functions of I1,…,InI_{1},\ldots,I_{n}, each nondecreasing in the priorities of its interval’s cells, are negatively associated, and so are their almost-sure limits as δ→0\delta\to 0, such as the largest age or the total age of the arrivals in each interval. Mapping any such function of IjI_{j} to an Exp⁡(xj)\mathrm{Exp}(x_{j}) clock by a nonincreasing map with fresh randomness thus also yields an OCEC generator.

9.

The First-Age Poisson generator is an OCEC generator.

Proof.

Coordinates with xj=0x_{j}=0 have clocks Yj=∞Y_{j}=\infty, which follow Exp⁡(0)\mathrm{Exp}(0) by convention. We omit such coordinates since adjoining constants preserves negative association by the closure under independent unions (Lemma 3).

Recall that the input sequence and the corresponding intervals are fixed independently of the generator’s randomness. For each jj, A^​(Ij)\widehat{A}(I_{j}) has distribution function FxjF_{x_{j}}, which is continuous except for an atom of mass e−λ​xje^{-\lambda x_{j}} at zero (Lemma 7). Hence, the randomized probability integral transform in (3) makes UjU_{j} uniform on [0,1][0,1], so Yj=−logUj/xj∼Exp(xj)Y_{j}=-\log U_{j}/x_{j}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(x_{j}).

The intervals IjI_{j} are pairwise disjoint, so their first ages are negatively associated by Lemma 8. For every fixed VjV_{j}, UjU_{j} is nondecreasing in A^​(Ij)\widehat{A}(I_{j}), since FxjF_{x_{j}} is nondecreasing and e−λ​xj​Vj≤e−λ​xj=Fxj​(0)e^{-\lambda x_{j}}V_{j}\leq e^{-\lambda x_{j}}=F_{x_{j}}(0). Hence, each YjY_{j} is a nonincreasing map of A^​(Ij)\widehat{A}(I_{j}) with fresh randomness VjV_{j}, and the clocks are negatively associated by the closure under concordant monotone maps. ∎

Choice of λ\lambda.

The rest of the paper fixes λ=4.5\lambda=4.5, a rounded value that approximately optimizes the competitive ratios of all applications under our analysis.

4 Warm-Up: Unweighted Matching

This section applies OCEC to unweighted matching, the simplest setting for our analysis, which Sections 5 and 6 extend to Display Ads and AdWords. Our goal here is to present the analysis in its simplest form rather than to optimize the ratio. Ranking already achieves the optimal ratio 1−1/e1-1/e for this problem [33].

Consider a bipartite graph G=(ℐ,𝒥,E)G=(\mathcal{I},\mathcal{J},E). Offline vertices i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I} are given upfront, and online vertices j∈𝒥j\in\mathcal{J} arrive one at a time. When jj arrives, the algorithm observes its edges and immediately and irrevocably matches it to at most one neighbor. The objective is the number of matched offline vertices. We assume without loss of generality that every online vertex has at least one neighbor, since an online vertex without neighbors would be irrelevant. The optimal matching size is at most the value of the standard matching LP, and hence, by weak duality, at most the objective of any feasible solution to its dual:

maxy≥0\displaystyle\max_{y\geq 0}\quad ∑(i,j)∈Eyi​j\displaystyle\textstyle\sum_{(i,j)\in E}y_{ij} minα,β≥0\displaystyle\min_{\alpha,\beta\geq 0}\quad ∑i∈ℐαi+∑j∈𝒥βj\displaystyle\textstyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\alpha_{i}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\beta_{j}
s.t. ∑j:(i,j)∈Eyi​j≤1∀i∈ℐ\displaystyle\textstyle\sum_{j:(i,j)\in E}y_{ij}\leq 1\quad\forall i\in\mathcal{I} s.t. αi+βj≥1∀(i,j)∈E\displaystyle\alpha_{i}+\beta_{j}\geq 1\quad\forall(i,j)\in E
∑i:(i,j)∈Eyi​j≤1∀j∈𝒥\displaystyle\textstyle\sum_{i:(i,j)\in E}y_{ij}\leq 1\quad\forall j\in\mathcal{J}

We use yy for the LP variables and reserve xx for the algorithm’s allocation masses. An offline vertex ii’s total fractional allocation ∑j:(i,j)∈Exi​j\sum_{j:(i,j)\in E}x_{ij} may exceed 11, so xx need not be feasible for the matching LP. The same distinction applies to Display Ads and AdWords.

1.

With the parameter λ=4.5\lambda=4.5, Online Primal-Dual Allocation with First-Age Poisson OCEC in Section 4.3 is 0.5560.556-competitive for unweighted matching.

We first analyze OCEC rounding for a fixed sequence of fractional allocations, and then design the fractional allocation rule via an online primal-dual analysis to prove Theorem 1.

4.1 Matching Kernel

Fresh competitor process.

Fix fractional allocations, rounded by OCEC with the First-Age Poisson generator. Since an offline vertex ii is matched exactly when Si≠∅S_{i}\neq\varnothing, and Si↦𝟙{Si≠∅}S_{i}\mapsto\mathds{1}\{S_{i}\neq\varnothing\} is submodular, Lemma 6 shows that ii is unmatched with probability at most that of losing every comparison against fresh competing clocks of rates 1−xi​j1-x_{ij}. We track this probability one request at a time. We use this comparison process in all applications considered in this paper.

Ages as states.

Given the current age of ii’s generator, its future arrivals and competing clocks are independent of the past, so the age is the state of ii between requests. We describe this state by a measure ν\nu on ages, where ν⁡(H)\nu(H) denotes the probability that ii has lost every comparison so far and has current age in a measurable set HH. Initially, ν\nu is the stationary distribution π=Exp⁡(λ)\pi=\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda). Its total mass ν⁡([0,∞))\nu([0,\infty)) may be less than 11, so ν\nu need not be a probability measure.

Requests as transitions.

Consider a request xx, placed on [0,x)[0,x) of ii’s timeline so that A⁡(0)A(0) and A⁡(x)A(x) are the ages before and after it. Let YY be its clock. Given YY, ii loses to the fresh competing clock with probability 1−e−(1−x)​Y1-e^{-(1-x)Y}. The matching kernel 𝖬x\mathsf{M}_{x} maps the measure ν\nu of ages before the request to the measure after it:

(ν𝖬x)(H)≔∫𝐄[𝟙{A(x)∈H}(1−e−(1−x)​Y)|A(0)=a]ν(da).(\nu\mathsf{M}_{x})(H)\coloneqq\int\mathbf{E}\bigl[\mathds{1}\{A(x)\in H\}\bigl(1-e^{-(1-x)Y}\bigr)\bigm|A(0)=a\bigr]\,\nu(\mathrm{d}a).

A request x=0x=0 changes nothing, and ii always wins a request x=1x=1 since it then has no competitor; that is, ν​𝖬0=ν\nu\mathsf{M}_{0}=\nu and ν​𝖬1=0\nu\mathsf{M}_{1}=0.

For a bounded measurable function ff on ages, write ν​f≔∫f​𝑑ν\nu f\coloneqq\int f\,\mathrm{d}\nu, which is the expected value of ff at the current age, counting only outcomes in which ii has lost every comparison so far. Then, (ν​𝖬x)​f(\nu\mathsf{M}_{x})f is the same quantity after the request. We also let 𝖬x\mathsf{M}_{x} act on functions, so that 𝖬x​f\mathsf{M}_{x}f maps each initial age to this expected value. Formally,

(𝖬x​f)​(a)≔𝐄⁡[f⁡(A⁡(x))​(1−e−(1−x)​Y)|A⁡(0)=a].(\mathsf{M}_{x}f)(a)\coloneqq\mathbf{E}\bigl[f(A(x))\,\bigl(1-e^{-(1-x)Y}\bigr)\bigm|A(0)=a\bigr]. (4)

By Fubini’s theorem, (ν​𝖬x)​f=ν⁡(𝖬x​f)(\nu\mathsf{M}_{x})f=\nu(\mathsf{M}_{x}f), so we may write ν​𝖬x​f\nu\mathsf{M}_{x}f without ambiguity.

In matrix terms, 𝖬x\mathsf{M}_{x} is a substochastic transition matrix, measures are row vectors, and functions are column vectors. Applying kernels in sequence corresponds to consecutive requests.

Reachable measures.

For any offline vertex ii, applying the kernels of its requests in arrival order, starting from π\pi, yields νi≔π∏j:(i,j)∈E𝖬xi​j\nu_{i}\coloneqq\pi\prod_{j:(i,j)\in E}\mathsf{M}_{x_{ij}}. More generally, we call a measure reachable if it can be obtained by consecutively applying matching kernels to the stationary distribution π\pi.

The total mass νi​𝟏\nu_{i}\mathbf{1} is the probability that ii loses every comparison, which bounds the probability that ii is unmatched by the reduction above:

𝐏𝐫⁡[i​ is unmatched]≤νi​𝟏.\mathbf{Pr}[i\text{ is unmatched}]\leq\nu_{i}\mathbf{1}. (5)

Consequently, the expected matching size is at least ∑i(1−νi​𝟏)\sum_{i}(1-\nu_{i}\mathbf{1}).

We construct a potential function Γ\Gamma on ages. Our online primal-dual analysis tracks each offline vertex ii through the potential νi​Γ\nu_{i}\Gamma of its current measure νi\nu_{i}, with the potential Γ⋆=π​Γ\Gamma^{\star}=\pi\Gamma of the stationary distribution as the target competitive ratio.

Intuitively, the worst case for matching consists of a sequence of infinitesimal requests, so we derive Γ\Gamma from the limit of such requests. We define the infinitesimal generator of the matching kernel by setting, for each bounded and continuously differentiable function ff with bounded derivative,

(ℒ𝖬​f)​(a)≔limx↓0(𝖬x​f)​(a)−f⁡(a)x.(\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{M}}f)(a)\coloneqq\lim_{x\downarrow 0}\frac{(\mathsf{M}_{x}f)(a)-f(a)}{x}.

As derived in Section B.3, we have the following lemma.

To describe the infinitesimal-request age process explicitly, consider a small request xx at age aa, whose competing clock has rate 1−x≈11-x\approx 1. With probability about λ​x\lambda x, the request’s interval contains an arrival with age about aa. By Lemma 7, its clock is then Y≈λ​e−λ​aY\approx\lambda e^{-\lambda a}, so ii wins with probability about e−λ​e−λ​ae^{-\lambda e^{-\lambda a}}, and otherwise its age restarts near zero. OCS-based analyses of matching [4, 20] translate a bound g⁡(x)g(x) on the probability of remaining unmatched after total allocation xx into a competitive ratio of 1−∫0∞e−x​g​(x)​𝑑x1-\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-x}g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x. 4.3 Online Primal-Dual Algorithm and Analysis

The algorithm maintains dual variables αi\alpha_{i} and βj\beta_{j} alongside the rounding. To show that the algorithm is Γ⋆\Gamma^{\star}-competitive, it suffices to establish two properties:

  1. (1)

    Reverse weak duality: the expected matching size is at least ∑iαi+∑jβj\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}+\sum_{j}\beta_{j}.

  2. (2)

    Approximate dual feasibility: α,β≥0\alpha,\beta\geq 0, and αi+βj≥Γ⋆\alpha_{i}+\beta_{j}\geq\Gamma^{\star} for every edge (i,j)(i,j).

Then, (α/Γ⋆,β/Γ⋆)(\alpha/\Gamma^{\star},\beta/\Gamma^{\star}) is dual feasible, so by weak duality, the optimal matching size is at most (∑iαi+∑jβj)/Γ⋆(\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}+\sum_{j}\beta_{j})/\Gamma^{\star}, and thus at most 1/Γ⋆1/\Gamma^{\star} times the expected matching size.

The offline dual variable αi≔Γ⋆−νi​Γ\alpha_{i}\coloneqq\Gamma^{\star}-\nu_{i}\Gamma records the potential spent by ii from its initial value Γ⋆=π​Γ\Gamma^{\star}=\pi\Gamma. For an arriving online vertex jj, let νi\nu_{i} denote neighbor ii’s measure before the allocation. After allocating mass xi​jx_{ij} to ii, its offline dual becomes αi=Γ⋆−νi​𝖬xi​j​Γ\alpha_{i}=\Gamma^{\star}-\nu_{i}\mathsf{M}_{x_{ij}}\Gamma. Thus, approximate dual feasibility requires βj≥νi​𝖬xi​j​Γ\beta_{j}\geq\nu_{i}\mathsf{M}_{x_{ij}}\Gamma for every neighbor ii. This motivates a water-filling procedure. We refer to νi​𝖬xi​j​Γ\nu_{i}\mathsf{M}_{x_{ij}}\Gamma as ii’s offer to jj. Starting from xi​j=0x_{ij}=0, we continuously allocate jj to neighbors with the largest current offers, splitting allocation among tied neighbors to keep their offers equal. All neighbors receiving positive allocation then have the same maximum final offer. After water filling, each neighbor ii contributes xi​j​νi​𝖬xi​j​Γx_{ij}\nu_{i}\mathsf{M}_{x_{ij}}\Gamma to βj\beta_{j}, using its final offer. Since the allocated masses sum to 11, βj\beta_{j} equals the maximum final offer and satisfies the required inequalities.

We need three lemmas about the reachable measures, the potential, and how they interact with the matching kernel. We give only proof sketches for two of them below, since all three follow from the stronger Display Ads lemmas stated in Section 5, which we prove in Appendix B.

11.

The tail bound says that conditioning on losing every comparison favors older ages relative to π\pi. Proof of Theorem 1.

We verify the two required properties of online primal-dual analysis.

Reverse weak duality.  Consider the arrival of jj, and let νi\nu_{i} be the measure of each neighbor ii before it. The request xi​jx_{ij} increases αi\alpha_{i} by νi​Γ−νi​𝖬xi​j​Γ\nu_{i}\Gamma-\nu_{i}\mathsf{M}_{x_{ij}}\Gamma and contributes xi​j​νi​𝖬xi​j​Γx_{ij}\nu_{i}\mathsf{M}_{x_{ij}}\Gamma to βj\beta_{j}, while it decreases νi​𝟏\nu_{i}\mathbf{1} by νi​𝟏−νi​𝖬xi​j​𝟏\nu_{i}\mathbf{1}-\nu_{i}\mathsf{M}_{x_{ij}}\mathbf{1}. By Lemma 13, the decrease is at least the dual increase. Summing over all requests, with each νi\nu_{i} starting at π\pi and each αi\alpha_{i} at zero, the final values satisfy ∑i(1−νi​𝟏)≥∑iαi+∑jβj\sum_{i}(1-\nu_{i}\mathbf{1})\geq\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}+\sum_{j}\beta_{j}, and (5) bounds the left side by the expected matching size.

Approximate dual feasibility.  By Lemma 12, νi​𝖬x​Γ\nu_{i}\mathsf{M}_{x}\Gamma is continuous and nonincreasing in xx, so water filling is well defined and each αi\alpha_{i} is nondecreasing from 00. 5 Display Ads

We next extend the analysis to Display Ads, or edge-weighted matching with free disposal. In this problem, advertisers i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I} are given upfront, and impressions j∈𝒥j\in\mathcal{J} arrive one at a time. On the arrival of jj, the algorithm observes the non-negative weights (wi​j)i∈ℐ(w_{ij})_{i\in\mathcal{I}} and immediately allocates jj to at most one advertiser. Advertisers have free disposal, so the value of advertiser ii is the maximum weight maxj∈Si⁡wi​j\max_{j\in S_{i}}w_{ij} among the impressions SiS_{i} assigned to it, and zero if SiS_{i} is empty. The objective is to maximize the total value of all advertisers. The offline optimum is the weight of a maximum-weight matching. Hence, the standard fractional benchmark and dual are

maxy≥0\displaystyle\max_{y\geq 0}\quad ∑i∈ℐ∑j∈𝒥wi​j​yi​j\displaystyle\textstyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}w_{ij}y_{ij} minα,β≥0\displaystyle\min_{\alpha,\beta\geq 0}\quad ∑i∈ℐαi+∑j∈𝒥βj\displaystyle\textstyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\alpha_{i}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\beta_{j}
s.t. ∑j∈𝒥yi​j≤1∀i∈ℐ\displaystyle\textstyle\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}y_{ij}\leq 1\quad\forall i\in\mathcal{I} s.t. αi+βj≥wi​j∀i∈ℐ,j∈𝒥\displaystyle\alpha_{i}+\beta_{j}\geq w_{ij}\quad\forall i\in\mathcal{I},\ j\in\mathcal{J}
∑i∈ℐyi​j≤1∀j∈𝒥.\displaystyle\textstyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}y_{ij}\leq 1\quad\forall j\in\mathcal{J}.

We use the same First-Age Poisson generators, matching kernel, and potential function as in Section 4. We now track a separate age measure for each advertiser ii at each weight level w≥0w\geq 0. Although this requires additional ideas, we retain the warm-up’s competitive ratio.

With the parameter λ=4.5\lambda=4.5, Online Primal-Dual Allocation with First-Age Poisson OCEC in Section 5.4 is 0.5560.556-competitive for Display Ads.

5.1 Analysis via Weight Levels

Fix an advertiser ii and a weight level w≥0w\geq 0. Let 𝒥i​(w)≔{j∈𝒥:wi​j≥w}\mathcal{J}_{i}(w)\coloneqq\{j\in\mathcal{J}:w_{ij}\geq w\} denote the set of online impressions with weight at least ww for advertiser ii. We say that level ww is covered if ii receives at least one impression in 𝒥i​(w)\mathcal{J}_{i}(w). An advertiser whose best impression has weight vv covers exactly the levels 0<w≤v0<w\leq v, so

maxj∈Siwi​j=∫0∞𝟙{Si∩𝒥i(w)≠∅}dw.\max_{j\in S_{i}}w_{ij}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathds{1}\{S_{i}\cap\mathcal{J}_{i}(w)\neq\varnothing\}\,\mathrm{d}w. (9)

Thus, at each fixed weight level, we seek to lower-bound the probability that the level is covered.

Age measures by weight levels.

We extend νi\nu_{i} to a family of age measures νi,w\nu_{i,w}, one for each weight level w≥0w\geq 0. Fix fractional allocations rounded by OCEC with the First-Age Poisson generator, and consider the fresh competitor process in Section 4. For each weight level ww, the function S↦𝟙​{∃j∈S:wi​j≥w}S\mapsto\mathds{1}\{\exists j\in S:w_{ij}\geq w\} is submodular. Thus, Lemma 6 bounds the probability that advertiser ii receives no impression of weight at least ww by the probability of losing every comparison with wi​j≥ww_{ij}\geq w against fresh clocks Zj∼Exp⁡(1−xi​j)Z_{j}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1-x_{ij}). We again track this probability through each νi,w\nu_{i,w} one request at a time, keeping ii’s generator and removing mass only for outcomes in which ii wins an impression with wi​j≥ww_{ij}\geq w.

5.2 Gap Kernel

An impression with wi​j<ww_{ij}<w cannot cover level ww, so its request removes no mass from νi,w\nu_{i,w}. Nevertheless, the request advances the generator’s internal time by xi​jx_{ij} and evolves the age measure. We describe this evolution by a gap kernel.

The age A⁡(t)A(t) increases at unit rate and resets to zero at each rate-λ\lambda Poisson arrival. For any bounded measurable function ff, define the gap kernel by

(𝖦t​f)​(a)≔𝐄⁡[f⁡(A⁡(t))|A⁡(0)=a],t≥0.(\mathsf{G}_{t}f)(a)\coloneqq\mathbf{E}\!\left[f(A(t))\,\middle|\,A(0)=a\right],\qquad t\geq 0.

We have 𝖦0=𝖨𝖽\mathsf{G}_{0}=\mathsf{Id}. It does not remove mass along the process, i.e., 𝖦t​𝟏=𝟏\mathsf{G}_{t}\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{1}, and the stationary age distribution is invariant, i.e., π​𝖦t=π\pi\mathsf{G}_{t}=\pi. The age dynamics give the following infinitesimal generator.

14.

For every bounded continuously differentiable function ff with bounded derivative,

(ℒ𝖦​f)​(a)=f′​(a)−λ​f​(a)+λ​f​(0).(\mathcal{L}_{\mathsf{G}}f)(a)=f^{\prime}(a)-\lambda f(a)+\lambda f(0).

The derivative at zero is the right derivative.

Proof.

Without arrivals, the age increases at unit rate, so the drift contributes f′​(a)f^{\prime}(a). With arrivals, which happen at rate λ\lambda, the age resets to zero, changing the function value by f⁡(0)−f⁡(a)f(0)-f(a). Combining these contributions gives the claimed generator. ∎

5.4 Online Primal-Dual Algorithm and Analysis

The algorithm maintains dual variables αi\alpha_{i} and βj\beta_{j} alongside the rounding. As in matching, Γ⋆\Gamma^{\star}-competitiveness follows by weak duality from two properties:

  1. (1)

    Reverse weak duality: the expected total value is at least ∑iαi+∑jβj\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}+\sum_{j}\beta_{j}.

  2. (2)

    Approximate dual feasibility: α,β≥0\alpha,\beta\geq 0 and αi+βj≥Γ⋆​wi​j\alpha_{i}+\beta_{j}\geq\Gamma^{\star}w_{ij} for every edge (i,j)(i,j).

The offline duals record spent potential across all weight levels:

αi,w≔Γ⋆−νi,w​Γ,αi≔∫0∞αi,w​𝑑w.\alpha_{i,w}\coloneqq\Gamma^{\star}-\nu_{i,w}\Gamma,\qquad\alpha_{i}\coloneqq\int_{0}^{\infty}\alpha_{i,w}\,\mathrm{d}w. (12)

They start at zero and never decrease after a request. Above all weights seen for ii, stationarity gives νi,w=π\nu_{i,w}=\pi and αi,w=0\alpha_{i,w}=0. The measures are constant between consecutive observed weights, so all level integrals reduce to finite sums, including the current weight as a breakpoint.

Let νi,w\nu_{i,w} be the measures when jj arrives. For a candidate mass x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1], let αi​(x)\alpha_{i}(x) denote advertiser ii’s offline dual after applying (10) once with mass xx. Let αi,w​(x)\alpha_{i,w}(x) denote the corresponding offline dual at weight level ww. Approximate dual feasibility requires βj≥Γ⋆​wi​j−αi​(xi​j)\beta_{j}\geq\Gamma^{\star}w_{ij}-\alpha_{i}(x_{ij}) for every advertiser ii. We therefore define advertiser ii’s offer per unit of allocation to βj\beta_{j} as

Γ⋆​wi​j−αi​(x)=∫0wi​jνi,w​𝖬x​Γ​𝑑w−∫wi​j∞(Γ⋆−νi,w​𝖦x​Γ)​𝑑w.\Gamma^{\star}w_{ij}-\alpha_{i}(x)=\int_{0}^{w_{ij}}\nu_{i,w}\mathsf{M}_{x}\Gamma\,\mathrm{d}w-\int_{w_{ij}}^{\infty}\bigl(\Gamma^{\star}-\nu_{i,w}\mathsf{G}_{x}\Gamma\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}w. (13)

The first term sums the remaining potential at weight levels lower than wi​jw_{ij}; the second accounts for the offline dual at higher weight levels. When all weights are one, this reduces to the offer νi​𝖬x​Γ\nu_{i}\mathsf{M}_{x}\Gamma for matching. Starting from xi​j=0x_{ij}=0, we continuously allocate jj to advertisers with the largest positive offers, splitting allocation among tied advertisers to keep their offers equal, until jj is fully allocated or no positive offer remains. By Lemma 17, each offer is continuous and nonincreasing in the allocation, so the water-filling procedure is well defined. Each advertiser receiving positive allocation has the maximum final offer. If jj is not fully allocated, all final offers are nonpositive, and those of advertisers receiving positive allocation are zero. Thus, setting βj\beta_{j} to the maximum final offer or zero, whichever is larger, gives

βj=∑ixi​j​(Γ⋆​wi​j−αi​(xi​j)).\beta_{j}=\sum_{i}x_{ij}\bigl(\Gamma^{\star}w_{ij}-\alpha_{i}(x_{ij})\bigr).
Proof of Theorem 2.

We verify the two required properties.

6 AdWords

In the AdWords problem, advertisers i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I} have budgets Bi>0B_{i}>0, and impressions j∈𝒥j\in\mathcal{J} arrive online. On the arrival of impression j∈𝒥j\in\mathcal{J}, the algorithm observes bids (bi​j)i∈ℐ(b_{ij})_{i\in\mathcal{I}} and immediately allocates jj to at most one advertiser. Recall that SiS_{i} is the set of impressions allocated to ii. The revenue from advertiser ii is min⁡{Bi,∑j∈Sibi​j}\min\{B_{i},\sum_{j\in S_{i}}b_{ij}\}. Thus, if a bid exceeding the remaining budget is allocated, it only contributes the remaining budget in revenue. Hence, we may assume 0≤bi​j≤Bi0\leq b_{ij}\leq B_{i}.

The optimal revenue is at most the optimal objectives of the following LP and its dual:

maxy≥0\displaystyle\max_{y\geq 0} ∑i∈ℐ∑j∈𝒥bi​j​yi​j\displaystyle\textstyle\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}b_{ij}y_{ij} minα,β≥0\displaystyle\qquad\min_{\alpha,\beta\geq 0} ∑i∈ℐBi​αi+∑j∈𝒥βj\displaystyle\textstyle\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}B_{i}\alpha_{i}+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\beta_{j} (14)
s.t.\displaystyle\text{s.t.} ∑j∈𝒥bi​j​yi​j≤Bi∀i∈ℐ\displaystyle\textstyle\displaystyle\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}}b_{ij}y_{ij}\leq B_{i}\quad\forall i\in\mathcal{I} s.t.\displaystyle\qquad\text{s.t.} bi​j​αi+βj≥bi​j∀i,j,\displaystyle b_{ij}\alpha_{i}+\beta_{j}\geq b_{ij}\quad\forall i,j,
∑i∈ℐyi​j≤1∀j∈𝒥.\displaystyle\textstyle\displaystyle\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}y_{ij}\leq 1\quad\forall j\in\mathcal{J}.

Write LP\mathrm{LP} for the optimum of this relaxation. As in the preceding sections, yi​jy_{ij} denotes a benchmark variable and xi​jx_{ij} denotes the fractional allocation passed to rounding.

Unlike in the matching setting, allocating an impression to an advertiser may not fully saturate their budget. Hence, the state space becomes more complex than just the age distribution. To manage this, we will separately track “small bids,” which are less than half the advertiser’s budget, and “large bids,” which are at least half.

For each pair (i,j)(i,j) with a small bid, advertiser ii competes for impression jj using a fresh exponential clock. Because these bids are small, this use of independent clocks already gives an improvement over the 1/21/2-competitive baseline analysis. For pairs with large bids, we obtain the clock from the advertiser’s First-Age Poisson generator. Winning two large bids exhausts an advertiser’s budget, so only histories with zero or one win on a large bid can contribute further revenue. This simplifies our state space, allowing us to conduct an analysis similar to Section 4. Combining the guarantees for both large and small bids, we prove the following theorem in the rest of this section.

3.

With λ=4.5\lambda=4.5, Online Primal-Dual Allocation with First-Age Poisson OCEC in Section 6.3 has expected revenue at least 0.530​LP0.530\,\mathrm{LP}.

6.1 Age Measures

Fresh competitor process.

Fix an advertiser ii and fractional allocations independent of the rounding randomness, and suppress ii from the notation. As in previous sections, we consider the evolution of its age process against fresh competing clocks. For the purpose of this process, we will always consider arriving bids normalized by the advertiser’s budget. Write b¯∈[0,1]\bar{b}\in[0,1] for a normalized bid (i.e. the ratio bi​jBi\frac{b_{ij}}{B_{i}} of the bid to the advertiser’s budget) and x∈[0,1]x\in[0,1] for its allocation mass. A bid is large if b¯≥1/2\bar{b}\geq 1/2 and small otherwise. For a large bid, we obtain a clock by sending mass xx to the advertiser’s First-Age Poisson generator. For a small bid, we draw a fresh Exp⁡(x)\mathrm{Exp}(x) clock without advancing the generator’s internal time.

By Lemma 3, independent unions preserve negative association, so the First-Age clocks for large bids and the independent clocks for small bids together form an OCEC generator. And the budget-additive revenue S↦min⁡{1,∑j∈Sb¯j}S\mapsto\min\{1,\sum_{j\in S}\bar{b}_{j}\} is submodular. Thus as before, Lemma 6 reduces the analysis to competition against fresh independent clocks Zj∼Exp⁡(1−xj)Z_{j}\sim\mathrm{Exp}(1-x_{j}). It suffices to lower-bound revenue, or equivalently upper-bound unused budget, in this comparison process.

The contribution of large bids.

Let AA be the current age, NN the number of large bids won so far, and RR the normalized remaining budget after accounting for large bids. Since every large bid is at least 1/21/2, we have R=0R=0 whenever N≥2N\geq 2. Thus, we only need to track age distributions for the states N=0N=0 and N=1N=1, which we will do using measures ν0\nu_{0} and ν1\nu_{1} respectively.

For a measurable age set HH, define

ν0​(H):=𝐏𝐫⁡[A∈H,N=0],ν1​(H):=𝐄⁡[R​ 1​{A∈H,N=1}].\nu_{0}(H):=\mathbf{Pr}[A\in H,\ N=0],\qquad\nu_{1}(H):=\mathbf{E}\!\left[R\,\mathds{1}\{A\in H,\ N=1\}\right].

The first measure is the surviving age measure of the matching problem. The second records the measure of trajectories with one win on a large bid, weighted by the budget still available. For example, a first win of bid 0.70.7 contributes weight 0.30.3 to ν1\nu_{1}; a second win on a large bid removes that trajectory entirely. This weighting records the effect of different large bids without keeping a separate measure for every remainder. Initially (ν0,ν1)=(π,0)(\nu_{0},\nu_{1})=(\pi,0), and at any point in the process, the expected remaining budget after accounting for large bids is (ν0+ν1)​𝟏=𝐄⁡[R](\nu_{0}+\nu_{1})\mathbf{1}=\mathbf{E}[R].

Recall the matching and gap kernels 𝖬x\mathsf{M}_{x} and 𝖦x\mathsf{G}_{x} from the previous sections. Define the win kernel 𝖶x:=𝖦x−𝖬x\mathsf{W}_{x}:=\mathsf{G}_{x}-\mathsf{M}_{x}. An impression with large bid b¯\bar{b} and mass xx updates the state (ν0,ν1)(\nu_{0},\nu_{1}) to (ν0′,ν1′)(\nu^{\prime}_{0},\nu^{\prime}_{1}) as follows:

ν0′=ν0​𝖬x,ν1′=ν1​𝖬x+(1−b¯)​ν0​𝖶x.\nu_{0}^{\prime}=\nu_{0}\mathsf{M}_{x},\qquad\nu_{1}^{\prime}=\nu_{1}\mathsf{M}_{x}+(1-\bar{b})\nu_{0}\mathsf{W}_{x}. (15)

Indeed, we know that ν0\nu_{0} updates according to the standard matching kernel, just as in the warm-up. For ν1\nu_{1}, existing mass updates according to 𝖬x\mathsf{M}_{x} since another large bid win would exhaust the budget, while winning mass from ν0\nu_{0} enters with weight 1−b¯1-\bar{b}.

The contribution of small bids.

Impressions with small bids leave both age measures fixed. We record only their normalized fractional load with the scalar quantity ss:

s:=∑j:b¯j<1/2b¯jxj.s:=\sum_{j:\,\bar{b}_{j}<1/2}\bar{b}_{j}x_{j}.

We seek to upper-bound the expected available budget as a function of ν0\nu_{0}, ν1\nu_{1}, and ss. Intuitively, the worst case for small bids comes from the Poissonized limit with many bids of size b¯j≈1/2\bar{b}_{j}\approx 1/2 with mass xjx_{j} close to 0. Assuming small bids contribute Pois⁡(2​s)\operatorname{Pois}(2s)-many wins of size 1/21/2, we get the unused-budget bound

U⁡(ν0,ν1,s):=e−2​s​((1+s)​ν0​𝟏+ν1​𝟏).U(\nu_{0},\nu_{1},s):=e^{-2s}\bigl((1+s)\nu_{0}\mathbf{1}+\nu_{1}\mathbf{1}\bigr). (16)

This expression comes from two cases. If no large bid is won, then Pois⁡(2​s)\operatorname{Pois}(2s) wins on bids of size 1/21/2 leave an expected remaining budget of e−2​s​(1+s)e^{-2s}(1+s), and this happens with probability ν0​𝟏\nu_{0}\mathbf{1}. If exactly one large bid is won, the Poisson comparison leaves budget RR when there are no Poisson wins, and zero otherwise. Since no Poisson win occurs with probability e−2​se^{-2s}, these histories contribute e−2​s​ν1​𝟏e^{-2s}\nu_{1}\mathbf{1} to the expected remaining budget. We make this comparison precise in the following lemma.

20.

At every input prefix, the advertiser’s expected normalized unused budget under the rounding is at most U⁡(ν0,ν1,s)U(\nu_{0},\nu_{1},s).

Proof.

By the OCEC comparison above, it suffices to consider fresh competitors. Let XX be the sum of the small bids won in that process. Its summands are independent b¯j​Bern⁡(xj)\bar{b}_{j}\operatorname{Bern}(x_{j}) variables, independent also of RR. Replacing each summand by 12​Pois⁡(2​b¯j​xj)\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{Pois}(2\bar{b}_{j}x_{j}) can only increase the expectation of a convex function of their sum. To see this, first replace it by 12​Bern⁡(2​b¯j​xj)\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{Bern}(2\bar{b}_{j}x_{j}) using the chord inequality on [0,1/2][0,1/2]. Then replace the Bernoulli variable by a Poisson variable of the same mean: at every nonnegative integer, a convex function lies above the line through its values at zero and one. Conditioning on the other summands justifies these replacements one at a time.

We write (z)+(z)_{+} for max⁡{z,0}\max\{z,0\}. Thus, for K∼Pois⁡(2​s)K\sim\operatorname{Pois}(2s) independent of RR,

𝐄[(R−X)+∣R]≤𝐄[(R−12K)+∣R]=e−2​s(R+s𝟏{R=1}).\mathbf{E}[(R-X)_{+}\mid R]\leq\mathbf{E}[(R-\tfrac{1}{2}K)_{+}\mid R]=e^{-2s}\bigl(R+s\mathbf{1}\{R=1\}\bigr).

The equality uses R∈{1}∪[0,1/2]R\in\{1\}\cup[0,1/2]: only K=0K=0 can leave a positive remainder when R≤1/2R\leq 1/2, while K=1K=1 leaves 1/21/2 when R=1R=1. Averaging and using 𝐄⁡[R]=(ν0+ν1)​𝟏\mathbf{E}[R]=(\nu_{0}+\nu_{1})\mathbf{1} and 𝐏𝐫[R=1]=ν0𝟏\mathbf{Pr}[R=1]=\nu_{0}\mathbf{1} gives (16). Impressions with large or small bids may be interleaved; their comparison outcomes are independent across the two groups, and the final remaining budget depends only on the sum of their winning bids. ∎

6.2 Potential of Reachable States

As in previous sections, we use a potential Γ\Gamma on the state (ν0,ν1,s)(\nu_{0},\nu_{1},s) to choose fractional allocations and dual variables. The competitive analysis requires nonnegativity, continuity, monotonicity, and an accounting inequality for every reachable state.

We assign an age-value function to each of the two measures and define

Γ⁡(ν0,ν1,s):=ν0​Γ0,s+ν1​Γ1,s,ΓAW⋆:=Γ⁡(π,0,0).\Gamma(\nu_{0},\nu_{1},s):=\nu_{0}\Gamma_{0,s}+\nu_{1}\Gamma_{1,s},\qquad\Gamma^{\star}_{\mathrm{AW}}:=\Gamma(\pi,0,0). (17)

Here Γ0,s\Gamma_{0,s} assigns potential to histories with no large bid won, while Γ1,s\Gamma_{1,s} assigns potential per unit of normalized budget remaining after one large bid is won. Both depend on ss, since small-bid load reduces the opportunity for future revenue. They replace the single age-value function Γ\Gamma used in matching. Our primal-dual analysis certifies competitive ratio ΓAW⋆\Gamma^{\star}_{\mathrm{AW}}.

A state is reachable if it is obtained from (π,0,0)(\pi,0,0) by applying (15) to impressions with large bids and s←s+b¯​xs\leftarrow s+\bar{b}x to impressions with small bids. For one such update, abbreviate the before and after values by U,ΓU,\Gamma and U′,Γ′U^{\prime},\Gamma^{\prime}. The required accounting for our primal-dual analysis is

U−U′⏟credited primal gain≥Γ−Γ′⏟offline dual increase+b¯​x​Γ′⏟online dual contribution.\underbrace{\vphantom{\big|}U-U^{\prime}}_{\text{credited primal gain}}\geq\underbrace{\vphantom{\big|}\Gamma-\Gamma^{\prime}}_{\text{offline dual increase}}+\underbrace{\vphantom{\big|}\bar{b}x\,\Gamma^{\prime}}_{\text{online dual contribution}}. (18)

This is the warm-up’s inequality with the online contribution scaled by the normalized bid b¯\bar{b}.

The following lemma summarizes the properties needed to prove Theorem 3. Section 6.4 describes the finite LP used to find this potential, and Appendix C proves the lemma.

21.

  1. 1.

    Γ0,s​(a)\Gamma_{0,s}(a) and Γ1,s​(a)\Gamma_{1,s}(a) are jointly continuous in (a,s)(a,s), continuously differentiable and bounded in aa for each fixed ss, and locally Lipschitz in ss uniformly over aa (hence locally absolutely continuous in ss).

    1. (a)

      (Accounting) U−U′≥Γ−Γ′+b¯​x​Γ′U-U^{\prime}\geq\Gamma-\Gamma^{\prime}+\bar{b}x\Gamma^{\prime}.

6.3 Online Primal-Dual Algorithm and Analysis

The algorithm maintains dual variables αi\alpha_{i} and βj\beta_{j} alongside the rounding. As in the previous sections, it suffices to prove:

  1. (1)

    Reverse weak duality: the expected revenue is at least ∑iBi​αi+∑jβj\sum_{i}B_{i}\alpha_{i}+\sum_{j}\beta_{j}.

  2. (2)

    Approximate dual feasibility: α,β≥0\alpha,\beta\geq 0, and bi​j​αi+βj≥ΓAW⋆​bi​jb_{ij}\alpha_{i}+\beta_{j}\geq\Gamma_{\mathrm{AW}}^{\star}b_{ij} for every pair (i,j)(i,j).

Then, (α/ΓAW⋆,β/ΓAW⋆)(\alpha/\Gamma_{\mathrm{AW}}^{\star},\beta/\Gamma_{\mathrm{AW}}^{\star}) is dual feasible. Together with the first property, weak duality then implies that the expected revenue is at least ΓAW⋆\Gamma_{\mathrm{AW}}^{\star} times the LP optimum.

The dual variables follow the potential. For each advertiser ii, write

Γi:=Γ⁡(νi,0,νi,1,si),αi:=ΓAW⋆−Γi.\Gamma_{i}:=\Gamma(\nu_{i,0},\nu_{i,1},s_{i}),\qquad\alpha_{i}:=\Gamma_{\mathrm{AW}}^{\star}-\Gamma_{i}.

Thus the offline dual αi\alpha_{i} records the potential spent from its initial value, and its contribution to the dual objective is Bi​αiB_{i}\alpha_{i}.

For an arriving impression jj, let b¯i​j=bi​j/Bi\bar{b}_{ij}=b_{ij}/B_{i} and hold each advertiser’s incoming state fixed. Write Γi(j)​(t)\Gamma_{i}^{(j)}(t) for its potential after a single request of normalized bid b¯i​j\bar{b}_{ij} and mass t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1]. For a large bid, apply (15) while keeping sis_{i} fixed. For a small bid, keep the age measures fixed and replace sis_{i} by si+b¯i​j​ts_{i}+\bar{b}_{ij}t. After allocating a fraction xi​jx_{ij} of impression jj to advertiser ii, its offline dual becomes αi=ΓAW⋆−Γi(j)​(xi​j)\alpha_{i}=\Gamma_{\mathrm{AW}}^{\star}-\Gamma_{i}^{(j)}(x_{ij}). Thus, approximate dual feasibility requires

βj≥bi​j​(ΓAW⋆−αi)=bi​j​Γi(j)​(xi​j)\beta_{j}\geq b_{ij}\bigl(\Gamma_{\mathrm{AW}}^{\star}-\alpha_{i}\bigr)=b_{ij}\Gamma_{i}^{(j)}(x_{ij})

for every advertiser ii. We therefore define advertiser ii’s offer per unit of allocation to βj\beta_{j} as bi​j​Γi(j)​(t)b_{ij}\Gamma_{i}^{(j)}(t). Starting from xi​j=0x_{ij}=0, we continuously allocate jj to advertisers with the largest current offers, splitting allocation among tied advertisers to keep their offers equal, until ∑ixi​j=1\sum_{i}x_{ij}=1. We set βj\beta_{j} to the maximum final offer to satisfy the required inequalities. Every advertiser receiving positive allocation has this offer. Since the allocated masses sum to 11, we have

βj=maxi⁡bi​j​Γi(j)​(xi​j)=∑ixi​j​bi​j​Γi(j)​(xi​j).\beta_{j}=\max_{i}b_{ij}\Gamma_{i}^{(j)}(x_{ij})=\sum_{i}x_{ij}b_{ij}\Gamma_{i}^{(j)}(x_{ij}).

The incoming states remain fixed throughout water filling; only the final chosen requests update them. Lemma 21 supplies both the accounting inequality and the continuity and monotonicity of the offers required for water filling.

Proof of Theorem 3.

We verify the two required properties of online primal-dual analysis.

Reverse weak duality.  Consider the arrival of impression jj. For advertiser ii, let UiU_{i} and Γi\Gamma_{i} denote the upper bound on its normalized unused budget and its remaining potential before the request, and let Ui′U_{i}^{\prime} and Γi′\Gamma_{i}^{\prime} denote the corresponding values afterward. The request xi​jx_{ij} increases αi\alpha_{i} by Γi−Γi′\Gamma_{i}-\Gamma_{i}^{\prime} and contributes xi​j​bi​j​Γi′=xi​j​bi​j​Γi(j)​(xi​j)x_{ij}b_{ij}\Gamma_{i}^{\prime}=x_{ij}b_{ij}\Gamma_{i}^{(j)}(x_{ij}) to βj\beta_{j}, while it decreases Bi​UiB_{i}U_{i} by Bi​(Ui−Ui′)B_{i}(U_{i}-U_{i}^{\prime}). By Lemma 20, the expected revenue is at least the left-hand side.

Approximate dual feasibility.  By Lemma 21, the offers bi​j​Γi(j)​(xi​j)b_{ij}\Gamma_{i}^{(j)}(x_{ij}) are continuous and nonincreasing in the allocation, so water filling is well defined and each αi\alpha_{i} is nondecreasing from 00. Moreover, βj≥0\beta_{j}\geq 0 since the potentials are nonnegative. By definition, immediately after processing impression jj, βj=maxi⁡bi​j​Γi′=maxi⁡bi​j​(ΓAW⋆−αi).\beta_{j}=\max_{i}b_{ij}\Gamma_{i}^{\prime}=\max_{i}b_{ij}\bigl(\Gamma_{\mathrm{AW}}^{\star}-\alpha_{i}\bigr). Hence bi​j​αi+βj≥ΓAW⋆​bi​jb_{ij}\alpha_{i}+\beta_{j}\geq\Gamma_{\mathrm{AW}}^{\star}b_{ij} for every ii, and these inequalities persist since αi\alpha_{i} never decreases. ∎

6.4 Choosing the Potential in Lemma 21

Here, we outline how we find the explicit potential function in Lemma 21 while optimizing for the competitive ratio.

The optimization problem.

Fix λ=9/2\lambda=9/2 and an advertiser with budget one. We seek age-value functions Γ0,s\Gamma_{0,s} and Γ1,s\Gamma_{1,s} defining

Γ⁡(ν0,ν1,s)=ν0​Γ0,s+ν1​Γ1,s.\Gamma(\nu_{0},\nu_{1},s)=\nu_{0}\Gamma_{0,s}+\nu_{1}\Gamma_{1,s}.

Their initial value ρ=Γ⁡(π,0,0)\rho=\Gamma(\pi,0,0) is the competitive ratio in the primal–dual analysis. We therefore leave ρ\rho free and ask for the largest value compatible with the other properties of Lemma 21:

maximize\displaystyle\text{maximize} ρ=π​Γ0,0\displaystyle\rho=\pi\Gamma_{0,0} (19)
subject to\displaystyle\text{subject to} Γ≥0,Γ′≤Γ,\displaystyle\Gamma\geq 0,\qquad\Gamma^{\prime}\leq\Gamma,
U−U′≥Γ−Γ′+b¯​x​Γ′.\displaystyle U-U^{\prime}\geq\Gamma-\Gamma^{\prime}+\bar{b}x\Gamma^{\prime}.

The constraints range over every reachable state (ν0,ν1,s)(\nu_{0},\nu_{1},s) and every normalized request (b¯,x)(\bar{b},x), where Γ′\Gamma^{\prime} and U′U^{\prime} denote the values after that request. We also require the regularity and monotonicity in request mass stated in the lemma. Even if we omit the regularity conditions, the above formulation already poses three challenges for numerical optimization:

  1. 1.

    Our solution space is infinite dimensional (namely, functions of age and small-bid load).

  2. 2.

    Constraints are given by reachable states (ν0,ν1,s)(\nu_{0},\nu_{1},s), which are implicitly defined.

  3. 3.

    There are infinitely many constraints given by each reachable state and each request.

We will address each of these challenges in turn, reducing our optimization problem to a finite LP whose candidate solutions can then be verified over all states and requests.

Reducing to finite variables.

We first simplify the optimization space by restricting the form of our functions. Since unused-budget UU already contains the factor e−2​se^{-2s}, we will factor it out of our unknown functions. Let z=e−λ​az=e^{-\lambda a} and write

Γ0,s(a)=e−2​sFs(z),Γ1,s(a)=e−2​sGs(z),Γ⁡(ν0,ν1,s)=e−2​s​(ν0​Fs+ν1​Gs).\begin{gathered}\Gamma_{0,s}(a)=e^{-2s}F_{s}(z),\qquad\Gamma_{1,s}(a)=e^{-2s}G_{s}(z),\\ \Gamma(\nu_{0},\nu_{1},s)=e^{-2s}(\nu_{0}F_{s}+\nu_{1}G_{s}).\end{gathered} (20)

The change of variables from age aa to zz gives a bounded domain: z=1z=1 is age zero, while z=0z=0 is the limit of very old ages. We use the same notation for an age measure and its image under this change of coordinates. In particular, π=Exp⁡(λ)\pi=\mathrm{Exp}(\lambda) becomes the uniform measure on [0,1][0,1], so the objective is simply ρ=∫01F0​(z)​𝑑z\rho=\int_{0}^{1}F_{0}(z)\,\mathrm{d}z.

We choose a polynomial degree dd for our functions and set “load knots” 0=s0<⋯<sK=S0=s_{0}<\cdots<s_{K}=S to discretize the space of the small-bid load ss. We use the Bernstein basis ℬjd​(z)=(dj)​zj​(1−z)d−j\mathcal{B}_{j}^{d}(z)=\binom{d}{j}z^{j}(1-z)^{d-j} and write

Fsk​(z)=∑j=0dfk​j​ℬjd​(z),Gsk​(z)=∑j=0dgk​j​ℬjd​(z).F_{s_{k}}(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}f_{kj}\mathcal{B}_{j}^{d}(z),\qquad G_{s_{k}}(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}g_{kj}\mathcal{B}_{j}^{d}(z). (21)

This basis provides simple linear sufficient conditions for nonnegativity and monotonicity, as well as uniform bounds for verification. For example, nonnegative, nonincreasing Bernstein coefficients yield a nonnegative, nonincreasing polynomial on [0,1][0,1], allowing us to enforce these regularity conditions through linear inequalities. The objective also has a simple linear form

ρ=∫01F0​(z)​𝑑z=1d+1​∑j=0df0​j.\rho=\int_{0}^{1}F_{0}(z)\,\mathrm{d}z=\frac{1}{d+1}\sum_{j=0}^{d}f_{0j}.

Between knots, interpolate the coefficients linearly. Beyond the last knot, use

Gs=GS,Fs=FS+(s−S)h(s≥S),G_{s}=G_{S},\qquad F_{s}=F_{S}+(s-S)h\quad(s\geq S), (22)

where h⁡(z)=∑j=0dhj​ℬjd​(z)h(z)=\sum_{j=0}^{d}h_{j}\mathcal{B}_{j}^{d}(z) is another degree-dd polynomial. In this way, we cover all possible small-bid load values ss.

We will use θ\theta to represent the coefficient vector which consists of all fk​j,gk​jf_{kj},g_{kj} and the coefficients of hh. Both the potential and the objective are linear in θ\theta, so our optimization problem reduces to an LP in θ\theta. However, this LP still has infinitely many linear constraints, which we address next.

Relaxing reachable measures to explicit inequalities.

Before we can discretize our constraints, we must make the space of constraints explicit by relaxing the set of reachable states to those satisfying specific inequalities. These include the tail bounds introduced in Section 4, along with a signed-score inequality.

In addition to ν0\nu_{0} and ν1\nu_{1}, we define the measure σ=ν0+2​ν1\sigma=\nu_{0}+2\nu_{1}. Both ν0\nu_{0} and σ\sigma attach weights to histories that can only decrease when another large bid is won, giving the tail condition

a⟼eλ​a​η​([a,∞))is nondecreasing for ​η∈{ν0,σ}.a\longmapsto e^{\lambda a}\eta([a,\infty))\quad\text{is nondecreasing for }\eta\in\{\nu_{0},\sigma\}.

Let 𝒞λ\mathcal{C}_{\lambda} denote the cone of finite nonnegative absolutely continuous measures with the rescaled-tail property above.

However, these tail restrictions alone still allow adverse states. For example, for sufficiently large TT, the pair ν0=π|[T,∞)\nu_{0}=\pi|_{[T,\infty)}, ν1=0\nu_{1}=0 satisfies the tail condition even though all surviving mass is very old. As it turns out, such states are problematic for our optimization, despite not arising as reachable measures.55 5 Poisson arrivals can reset the age without producing a win on a large bid, so any nonzero reachable ν0\nu_{0} retains young surviving histories. Hence, the truncated stationary distribution π|[T,∞)\pi|_{[T,\infty)} is unreachable. Our potential assigns more value to older histories, reflecting better opportunities to win future large bids. However, small-bid rounding ignores age. Concentrating surviving mass at old ages can therefore increase the dual charges Γ−Γ′+b¯​x​Γ′\Gamma-\Gamma^{\prime}+\bar{b}x\Gamma^{\prime} without a corresponding increase in the revenue gain U−U′U-U^{\prime} from small bids, making accounting more restrictive. To fix this, we further introduce a signed score function HH, for which H⁡(e−λ​a)H(e^{-\lambda a}) is positive for small ages aa and negative for sufficiently large aa. We prove that all reachable measures ν0\nu_{0} have ν0​H≥0,\nu_{0}H\geq 0, ruling out these truncated tails.

Ultimately, the class of measures we consider is as follows. We will enforce our accounting inequality constraint on all pairs (ν0,ν1)(\nu_{0},\nu_{1}) satisfying

ν0,ν1≥0,ν0,ν0+2​ν1∈𝒞λ,ν0​H≥0.\nu_{0},\nu_{1}\geq 0,\qquad\nu_{0},\ \nu_{0}+2\nu_{1}\in\mathcal{C}_{\lambda},\qquad\nu_{0}H\geq 0. (23)

Every reachable state belongs to this class, so this only strengthens the constraints of our program.

Discretizing constraints.

Finally, we reduce our optimization problem to one with finitely many constraints. Nonnegativity and monotonicity follow from simple linear inequalities on the polynomial coefficients; the accounting constraint requires more work.

For fixed measures (ν0,ν1)(\nu_{0},\nu_{1}), polynomial bounds for b¯\bar{b} and interpolation between knots for ss reduce accounting to finitely many test families. The LP imposes these tests at finitely many values of xx; uniform bounds between test points then certify all request masses during verification.66 6 As in matching, small request masses require special care because the accounting slack vanishes at x=0x=0. For large bids, we divide the slack by xx and evaluate its limit at zero using the infinitesimal generator. For small bids, we verify a differential accounting inequality in the load ss and integrate it over the increment b¯​x\bar{b}x. The resulting LP tests have the form ν0​C0+ν1​C1≥0\nu_{0}C_{0}+\nu_{1}C_{1}\geq 0, where the costs C0,C1C_{0},C_{1} depend affinely on θ\theta.

The signed-score inequality also gives additional flexibility in each test. For any τ≥0\tau\geq 0, it suffices to show ν0​(C0−τ​H)+ν1​C1≥0\nu_{0}(C_{0}-\tau H)+\nu_{1}C_{1}\geq 0, since ν0​H≥0\nu_{0}H\geq 0. We can choose a different τ\tau for each test. After this adjustment, we need to satisfy these tests for all pairs (ν0,ν1)(\nu_{0},\nu_{1}) satisfying the tail bounds.

To do this, we replace each measure with a finite-dimensional sketch. Choose a partition 0=t0<⋯<tN=10=t_{0}<\cdots<t_{N}=1 in the transformed coordinate z=e−λ​az=e^{-\lambda a}. We abuse notation slightly and use νr\nu_{r}, for r∈{0,1}r\in\{0,1\}, to denote the image of the original age measure under this transformation. Replace this transformed measure by a sketch recording just its mass in each bucket:

yr​i=νr​((ti−1,ti]),r∈{0,1},1≤i≤N.y_{ri}=\nu_{r}((t_{i-1},t_{i}]),\qquad r\in\{0,1\},\quad 1\leq i\leq N.

To evaluate a test from this sketch, we bound C0−τ​HC_{0}-\tau H and C1C_{1} below by constants v0​iv_{0i} and v1​iv_{1i} throughout bucket ii. Then v⊤​yv^{\top}y is a lower bound on ν0​(C0−τ​H)+ν1​C1\nu_{0}(C_{0}-\tau H)+\nu_{1}C_{1}, regardless of how the mass is distributed inside each bucket. For measures with ν0​H≥0\nu_{0}H\geq 0, it therefore also lower-bounds the original accounting cost ν0​C0+ν1​C1\nu_{0}C_{0}+\nu_{1}C_{1}. Finer buckets can reduce this approximation loss.

The tail bounds from (23) translate into linear inequalities on cumulative bucket masses, which apply to both ν0\nu_{0} and ν0+2​ν1\nu_{0}+2\nu_{1}. Because the accounting inequality is homogeneous in the measures, we can normalize their total mass to one, and the sketches allowed by these tail constraints form a polytope

𝒴={y≥0:Ay≤0, 1⊤y=1},\mathcal{Y}=\{y\geq 0:Ay\leq 0,\ \mathbf{1}^{\top}y=1\},

By LP duality, the requirement v⊤​y≥0v^{\top}y\geq 0 for every y∈𝒴y\in\mathcal{Y} is equivalent to the existence of multipliers uu satisfying

u≥0,v+A⊤​u≥0.u\geq 0,\qquad v+A^{\top}u\geq 0.

These finite linear inequalities certify the test once the bucket bounds vr​iv_{ri} are valid.

7 Load Balancing

In this problem, machines i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I} are given upfront, and jobs j∈𝒥j\in\mathcal{J} arrive online one at a time. On the arrival of job jj, the algorithm observes the job size pi​j>0p_{ij}>0 on each machine ii; pi​j=∞p_{ij}=\infty if it is infeasible to process jj on machine ii. We assume every job has at least one feasible machine and use the convention ∞⋅0=0\infty\cdot 0=0. The algorithm then immediately assigns job jj to a machine. The objective is to minimize the total squared load

∑i∈ℐLi2,where ​Li=∑j∈Sipi​j,\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}L_{i}^{2},\quad\text{where }L_{i}=\sum_{j\in S_{i}}p_{ij}~,

recalling that SiS_{i} is the set of jobs assigned to machine ii.

Write ALG=∑i𝐄⁡[Li2]\operatorname{ALG}=\sum_{i}\mathbf{E}[L_{i}^{2}] for the algorithm’s expected objective, and OPT\operatorname{OPT} for the minimum objective of an offline integral assignment. Write Xi​j=𝟏{j∈Si}X_{ij}=\mathbf{1}\{j\in S_{i}\} for the allocation indicator.

4.

With the common rate λ=4.5\lambda=4.5, the algorithm in Section 7.3 is Γ\Gamma-competitive for minimizing squared loads on unrelated machines, where Γ=4.69\Gamma=4.69.

7.1 Convex Program Duality

We use the convex relaxation of [17], specialized to squared loads, and its dual. Let xi​j≥0x_{ij}\geq 0 be the fraction of job jj assigned to machine ii, and write xi=(xi​j)jx_{i}=(x_{ij})_{j}. We set xi​j=0x_{ij}=0 whenever pi​j=∞p_{ij}=\infty. For a job size p>0p>0 and a threshold p¯≥0\bar{p}\geq 0, define

∑jxi​j​min⁡{pi​j,p¯i}=p¯i.\sum_{j}x_{ij}\min\bigl\{p_{ij},\bar{p}_{i}\bigr\}=\bar{p}_{i}.

The convex program and its dual are

minx≥0\displaystyle\min_{x\geq 0}\quad ∑i𝒞i​(xi)\displaystyle\sum_{i}\mathcal{C}_{i}(x_{i}) maxα,β≥0\displaystyle\max_{\alpha,\beta\geq 0}\quad ∑jβj−∑iαi2\displaystyle\sum_{j}\beta_{j}-\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}^{2}
s.t. ∑ixi​j≥1∀j∈𝒥\displaystyle\sum_{i}x_{ij}\geq 1\quad\forall j\in\mathcal{J} s.t. βj≤Φ⁡(αi,pi​j)∀(i,j).\displaystyle\beta_{j}\leq\Phi(\alpha_{i};p_{ij})\quad\forall(i,j).

Writing γi=αi2\gamma_{i}=\alpha_{i}^{2} gives the convex form of the Fenchel dual, since γ↦Φ⁡(γ,p)\gamma\mapsto\Phi(\sqrt{\gamma};p) is concave. We use the square-root variables αi=γi\alpha_{i}=\sqrt{\gamma_{i}} to simplify notation in the competitive analysis.

Our dual is a restriction of the SDP dual used by [6]. The dual assignment in their analysis satisfies this restriction.77 7 In their notation, restrict vi​j=qi​j​eiv_{ij}=q_{ij}e_{i} to 0≤qi​j≤2​pi​j0\leq q_{ij}\leq\sqrt{2}p_{ij}, where eie_{i} is the unit vector for machine ii, as their analysis does. These bounds ensure all pairwise vector constraints. For fixed ν=2​α\nu=\sqrt{2}\alpha, maximizing each remaining constraint’s right-hand side gives qi​j=2​min⁡{pi​j,αi}q_{ij}=\sqrt{2}\min\{p_{ij},\alpha_{i}\} and yj≤Φ⁡(αi,pi​j)y_{j}\leq\Phi(\alpha_{i};p_{ij}). Identifying yj=βjy_{j}=\beta_{j} preserves the dual objective ∑jβj−∑iαi2\sum_{j}\beta_{j}-\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}^{2}. The improved competitive ratio comes from the First-Age Poisson rounding and its amortized analysis, rather than from a stronger relaxation.

22Relaxation and Weak Duality.

The primal program is a relaxation of load balancing. Consequently, every feasible dual solution satisfies

∑jβj−∑iαi2≤OPT.\sum_{j}\beta_{j}-\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}^{2}\leq\operatorname{OPT}.
Proof.

For any integral assignment and any fixed p¯\bar{p}, Φ⁡(p¯,p)\Phi(\bar{p};p) is convex in pp and vanishes at p=0p=0, so

∑j∈SiΦ⁡(p¯i,pi​j)−p¯i2≤Φ⁡(p¯i,Li)−p¯i2=Li2−(p¯i−Li)+2≤Li2.\sum_{j\in S_{i}}\Phi(\bar{p}_{i};p_{ij})-\bar{p}_{i}^{2}\leq\Phi(\bar{p}_{i};L_{i})-\bar{p}_{i}^{2}=L_{i}^{2}-(\bar{p}_{i}-L_{i})_{+}^{2}\leq L_{i}^{2}.

Equality holds at p¯i=Li\bar{p}_{i}=L_{i}, where Φ⁡(Li,pi​j)=2​Li​pi​j\Phi(L_{i};p_{ij})=2L_{i}p_{ij}, proving 𝒞i​(xi)=Li2\mathcal{C}_{i}(x_{i})=L_{i}^{2}. Since every integral assignment is feasible for the primal program, the program is a relaxation. Finally, for any feasible dual solution (α,β)(\alpha,\beta), the definition of 𝒞i\mathcal{C}_{i} gives 𝒞i​(xi)≥∑jxi​j​βj−αi2\mathcal{C}_{i}(x_{i})\geq\sum_{j}x_{ij}\beta_{j}-\alpha_{i}^{2}. Summing over machines in an optimal integral assignment proves the dual bound. ∎

7.2 Covariance Savings and Cost Accounting

Fix any machine ii. Write j∼ij\sim i if entry (i,j)(i,j) is passed to machine ii’s persistent First-Age Poisson generator. Let ti​(j)t_{i}(j) denote the internal time of machine ii’s correlated timeline immediately before job jj. For j∼ij\sim i, its request interval is Ii​j=[ti(j),ti(j)+xi​j)I_{ij}=[t_{i}(j),t_{i}(j)+x_{ij}). An independent entry uses a fresh Exp⁡(xi​j)\mathrm{Exp}(x_{ij}) clock and does not advance that timeline. The designation of an entry, as well as its mass xi​jx_{ij}, is independent of the sampled clocks. This section bounds the covariance savings from the entries correlated via OCEC.

23.

For every i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I} and j∈𝒥j\in\mathcal{J}, we have 𝐄⁡[Xi​j]=xi​j\mathbf{E}[X_{ij}]=x_{ij}. For every i∈ℐi\in\mathcal{I} and distinct j,k∈𝒥j,k\in\mathcal{J},

𝐄⁡[Xi​j​Xi​k]≤𝐄⁡[e−(1−xi​j)​Yi​j−(1−xi​k)​Yi​k]≤xi​j​xi​k.\mathbf{E}[X_{ij}X_{ik}]\leq\mathbf{E}\bigl[e^{-(1-x_{ij})Y_{ij}-(1-x_{ik})Y_{ik}}\bigr]\leq x_{ij}x_{ik}.
Proof.

The marginal identity follows by the exponential marginals, the independence of different offline objects’ OCEC generators, and the fact that ∑i′∈ℐxi′​j=1\sum_{i^{\prime}\in\mathcal{I}}x_{i^{\prime}j}=1. The pairwise bounds are immediate if either mass is zero or one. Otherwise, conditional on Yi​j=yY_{ij}=y and Yi​k=zY_{ik}=z, independence across offline objects and negative association on each other object give

𝐏𝐫[Xi​j=Xi​k=1∣Yi​j=y,Yi​k=z]\displaystyle\mathbf{Pr}[X_{ij}=X_{ik}=1\mid Y_{ij}=y,Y_{ik}=z] ≤∏i′≠i𝐏𝐫[Yi′​j>y]𝐏𝐫[Yi′​k>z]\displaystyle\leq\prod_{i^{\prime}\neq i}\mathbf{Pr}[Y_{i^{\prime}j}>y]\mathbf{Pr}[Y_{i^{\prime}k}>z]
=e−(1−xi​j)​y−(1−xi​k)​z.\displaystyle=e^{-(1-x_{ij})y-(1-x_{ik})z}.

Taking expectations gives the first inequality; negative association gives the second:

𝐄⁡[e−(1−xi​j)​Yi​j−(1−xi​k)​Yi​k]≤𝐄⁡[e−(1−xi​j)​Yi​j]​𝐄​[e−(1−xi​k)​Yi​k]=xi​j​xi​k.\mathbf{E}\bigl[e^{-(1-x_{ij})Y_{ij}-(1-x_{ik})Y_{ik}}\bigr]\leq\mathbf{E}\bigl[e^{-(1-x_{ij})Y_{ij}}\bigr]\mathbf{E}\bigl[e^{-(1-x_{ik})Y_{ik}}\bigr]=x_{ij}x_{ik}.

∎

Our algorithm in Section 7.3 ensures xi​j≤x¯=0.15x_{ij}\leq\overline{x}=0.15 for every entry (i,j)(i,j) passed to OCEC. We now quantify the pairwise covariance savings of such jobs on a machine.

25.

(25)
Proof.

By Lemma 23, averaging over the private uniforms gives

Write Aj=A^​(Ii​j)A_{j}=\widehat{A}(I_{ij}) and Ak=A^​(Ii​k)A_{k}=\widehat{A}(I_{ik}). Since DxD_{x} is nondecreasing, for any A≥0A\geq 0 we have

Dx(A)=Dx(0)+∫[0,∞)𝟏{A>a}dDx(a).D_{x}(A)=D_{x}(0)+\int_{[0,\infty)}\mathbf{1}\{A>a\}\,dD_{x}(a).

The corresponding condition at t′∈Ii​kt^{\prime}\in I_{ik} requires an empty interval of length max⁡{b,t′−ti​(k)}\max\{b,t^{\prime}-t_{i}(k)\}.
