On incompatible pairs, the later empty interval has length bb. Integrating the product densities over these pairs therefore gives

𝐏𝐫[A^(Ii​j)>a]𝐏𝐫[A^(Ii​k)>b]−𝐏𝐫[A^(Ii​j)>a,A^(Ii​k)>b]\displaystyle\mathbf{Pr}[\widehat{A}(I_{ij})>a]\mathbf{Pr}[\widehat{A}(I_{ik})>b]-\mathbf{Pr}[\widehat{A}(I_{ij})>a,\widehat{A}(I_{ik})>b]
=λ2∫Ii​j∫Ii​ke−λ⁡(max⁡{a,t−ti​(j)}+b)𝟏{t′−t≤b}dt′dt.\displaystyle=\lambda^{2}\int_{I_{ij}}\int_{I_{ik}}e^{-\lambda(\max\{a,t-t_{i}(j)\}+b)}\mathbf{1}\{t^{\prime}-t\leq b\}\,dt^{\prime}\,dt.

7.3 Online Primal-Dual Algorithm

Instead of setting αi\alpha_{i} to be the maximizing threshold p¯i\bar{p}_{i}, we maintain it heuristically as half the expected load. That is, we let

αi=ℓi2,\alpha_{i}=\frac{\ell_{i}}{2}~,

where ℓi\ell_{i} is the expected load of machine ii from jobs seen so far.

Correspondingly, we use Φ⁡(ℓi/2,pi​j)\Phi(\ell_{i}/2;p_{ij}) as a surrogate marginal price. Upon the arrival of job jj, choose the fractional allocation by water filling with these prices:

(xi​j)i∈arg​minxi≥0,∑ixi=1∑i∫0xiΦ(ℓi+pi​j​u2;pi​j)du.(x_{ij})_{i}\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{x_{i}\geq 0,\ \sum_{i}x_{i}=1}\sum_{i}\int_{0}^{x_{i}}\Phi\!\left(\frac{\ell_{i}+p_{ij}u}{2};p_{ij}\right)\,du. (26)

After allocating job jj, we have ℓi+=ℓi+pi​j​xi​j\ell_{i}^{+}=\ell_{i}+p_{ij}x_{ij}.

Each feasible machine’s price is continuous and strictly increasing, so the objective is strictly convex and the fractional allocation is unique. At a minimizer, positive coordinates have a common endpoint price, and zero coordinates have no smaller price. Set βj\beta_{j} to this common price, equivalently

βj=mini⁡Φ⁡(ℓi+2,pi​j)=∑ixi​j​Φ​(ℓi+2,pi​j).\beta_{j}=\min_{i}\Phi\!\left(\frac{\ell_{i}^{+}}{2};p_{ij}\right)=\sum_{i}x_{ij}\Phi\!\left(\frac{\ell_{i}^{+}}{2};p_{ij}\right).

This choice satisfies the dual constraints for job jj, and monotonicity of the expected loads preserves all previous dual constraints.

Choosing the Rounding Rule.

For a positive xi​j>0x_{ij}>0, independent rounding increases ALG¯\overline{\operatorname{ALG}} by pi​j2​xi​j+2​pi​j​ℓi​xi​jp_{ij}^{2}x_{ij}+2p_{ij}\ell_{i}x_{ij}, and increases the dual objective by xi​j​Φ​(ℓi+/2,pi​j)−((ℓi+)2−ℓi2)/4x_{ij}\Phi(\ell_{i}^{+}/2;p_{ij})-((\ell_{i}^{+})^{2}-\ell_{i}^{2})/4. We use independent rounding if the former is at most Γ0\Gamma_{0} times the latter, that is, if

pi​j2​xi​j+2​pi​j​ℓi​xi​j≤Γ0​(xi​j​Φ​(ℓi+2,pi​j)−(ℓi+)2−ℓi24),p_{ij}^{2}x_{ij}+2p_{ij}\ell_{i}x_{ij}\leq\Gamma_{0}\biggl(x_{ij}\Phi\!\left(\frac{\ell_{i}^{+}}{2};p_{ij}\right)-\frac{(\ell_{i}^{+})^{2}-\ell_{i}^{2}}{4}\biggr), (27)

and use OCEC otherwise. We choose

Γ0=4.573,\Gamma_{0}=4.573, (28)

slightly smaller than the final competitive ratio Γ=4.69\Gamma=4.69, to account for the loss from an auxiliary potential in the final competitive analysis.

The test depends only on the expected load, the job size, and the allocated mass. The following lemma ensures that correlated entries satisfy the mass bound required by Lemma 26.

Every entry with j∼ij\sim i satisfies xi​j<x¯x_{ij}<\overline{x}.

Proof.

Fix a positive entry (i,j)(i,j) and let b=12+2Γ0∈(0,1)b=\frac{1}{2}+\frac{2}{\Gamma_{0}}\in(0,1). The formula for Φ\Phi gives

Φ⁡(ℓi+2,pi​j)≥pi​j2​(1−b2)+b​pi​j​ℓi+.\Phi\!\left(\frac{\ell_{i}^{+}}{2};p_{ij}\right)\geq p_{ij}^{2}(1-b^{2})+bp_{ij}\ell_{i}^{+}.

1Γ0−1+b2−(b−14)​xi​j≤1Γ0−1+b2−(b−14)​x¯<0\frac{1}{\Gamma_{0}}-1+b^{2}-\left(b-\frac{1}{4}\right)x_{ij}\leq\frac{1}{\Gamma_{0}}-1+b^{2}-\left(b-\frac{1}{4}\right)\overline{x}<0

7.4 Competitive Analysis

A correlated entry can incur a deficit before it generates covariance savings: the first correlated entry on a machine has Δi​j​(xi​j)=0\Delta_{ij}(x_{ij})=0, but fails (27). Savings from its interactions with later entries can compensate for this deficit, so we amortize the comparison across arrivals. [6] likewise aggregate covariance savings over groups of jobs.

28Amortized Cost Bound.

There is a potential Ψ\Psi with the following properties:

  1. 1.

    Initially, Ψ=0\Psi=0.

  2. 2.

    At every prefix,

    Ψ≤ν​∑iℓi2,ν=0.00539.\Psi\leq\nu\sum_{i}\ell_{i}^{2},\qquad\nu=0.00539.
  3. 3.

    For each arriving job jj, write DD for the current dual objective. Then

    ALG¯+−ALG¯≤Γ0​(D+−D+Ψ+−Ψ).\overline{\operatorname{ALG}}^{+}-\overline{\operatorname{ALG}}\leq\Gamma_{0}\bigl(D^{+}-D+\Psi^{+}-\Psi\bigr). (29)

Sum (29) over jobs and apply Lemma 27 and Corollary 1 to obtain

ALG≤ALG¯≤Γ0​(D+Ψ)≤Γ0​(OPT+Ψ),\operatorname{ALG}\leq\overline{\operatorname{ALG}}\leq\Gamma_{0}(D+\Psi)\leq\Gamma_{0}(\operatorname{OPT}+\Psi),

Ψ≤ν​∑iℓi2≤ν​ALG.\Psi\leq\nu\sum_{i}\ell_{i}^{2}\leq\nu\operatorname{ALG}.

Hence

ALG≤Γ01−Γ0​ν​OPT<4.69​OPT=Γ​OPT.\operatorname{ALG}\leq\frac{\Gamma_{0}}{1-\Gamma_{0}\nu}\,\operatorname{OPT}<4.69\,\operatorname{OPT}=\Gamma\,\operatorname{OPT}.

∎

Proof Sketch of Lemma 28.

For auxiliary values 0≤α~i≤αi0\leq\widetilde{\alpha}_{i}\leq\alpha_{i} defined below, set

Ψ=∑i(αi2−α~i2).\Psi=\sum_{i}(\alpha_{i}^{2}-\widetilde{\alpha}_{i}^{2}).

Ψ=∑i(αi+α~i)​(αi−α~i)≤∑iℓi​(αi−α~i).\Psi=\sum_{i}(\alpha_{i}+\widetilde{\alpha}_{i})(\alpha_{i}-\widetilde{\alpha}_{i})\leq\sum_{i}\ell_{i}(\alpha_{i}-\widetilde{\alpha}_{i}).

Thus, property 2 follows if αi−α~i≤ν​ℓi\alpha_{i}-\widetilde{\alpha}_{i}\leq\nu\ell_{i} for every machine at every prefix.

Recall that Δi​j​(x)\Delta_{ij}(x) is the covariance credit per unit of job size for a trial mass xx, right before processing job jj. Hence, Δi​j​(∞)\Delta_{ij}(\infty) captures the total remaining covariance credit from interactions between the existing correlated intervals and the future timeline, per unit of future job size. Here the current history stays fixed, and only the trial interval extends to infinity. We use a scaled, capped version of this remaining credit to define the gap αi−α~i\alpha_{i}-\widetilde{\alpha}_{i}. Cap each job size at half the expected load immediately before its arrival:

p~i​j=min⁡{pi​j,αi​(j)}=min⁡{pi​j,ℓi​(j)2}.\tilde{p}_{ij}=\min\{p_{ij},\alpha_{i}(j)\}=\min\Bigl\{p_{ij},\frac{\ell_{i}(j)}{2}\Bigr\}.

Each capped size is fixed upon arrival and remains unchanged thereafter. Replacing each earlier job size by its capped value gives

Δ~i​j​(x)=2​∑k<jk∼ip~i​k​∫Ii​k∫titi+xδ⁡(v−u)​𝑑v​𝑑u.\widetilde{\Delta}_{ij}(x)=2\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k<j\\ k\sim i\end{subarray}}\tilde{p}_{ik}\int_{I_{ik}}\int_{t_{i}}^{t_{i}+x}\delta(v-u)\,dv\,du.

Thus 0≤Δ~i​j​(x)≤Δi​j​(x)0\leq\widetilde{\Delta}_{ij}(x)\leq\Delta_{ij}(x). Set

α~i=αi−0.15​Δ~i​j​(∞).\widetilde{\alpha}_{i}=\alpha_{i}-0.15\,\widetilde{\Delta}_{ij}(\infty).

Capping the job sizes plays two roles. First, it keeps the remaining credit small relative to the current load, which bounds the potential and establishes the second property of the lemma. The high-level plan is to use both p~i​k≤αi​(k)\tilde{p}_{ik}\leq\alpha_{i}(k) and the increase pi​k​xi​k/2≥p~i​k​xi​k/2p_{ik}x_{ik}/2\geq\tilde{p}_{ik}x_{ik}/2 in αi\alpha_{i} caused by each allocation to constrain the history of capped sizes. These constraints yield a differential inequality for the cumulative capped load in the recent history. Integrating its solution against the covariance saving function bounds αi−α~i\alpha_{i}-\widetilde{\alpha}_{i} by a constant times the current load. Section D.2 certifies that this constant is below ν\nu by numerically bounding a single scalar integral.

Second, capping controls the cost of releasing earlier credit in the amortized comparison. When a correlated entry (i,j)(i,j) advances the timeline, interactions between earlier intervals and Ii​jI_{ij} no longer belong to the future timeline. Their removal decreases αi−α~i\alpha_{i}-\widetilde{\alpha}_{i} by 0.15​Δ~i​j​(xi​j)0.15\,\widetilde{\Delta}_{ij}(x_{ij}). We call this decrease releasing credit; it raises α~i\widetilde{\alpha}_{i}, reducing the increase in the auxiliary objective.

For example, preload 5050 machines to load 22 using jobs feasible on only one machine. Then present 3030 jobs with size 3​αi/23\alpha_{i}/2 on each machine ii, followed by one with size 5​αi/85\alpha_{i}/8, evaluating αi\alpha_{i} before each arrival. Water filling assigns mass 1/501/50 per machine, and all these entries fail (27). With the uncapped reserve, α~i=αi−0.15​Δi​j​(∞)\widetilde{\alpha}_{i}=\alpha_{i}-0.15\Delta_{ij}(\infty), the amortized comparison (29) fails on the final job. Here the cap reduces the earlier deposits by one third while leaving the final job’s deposit unchanged. Lowering the cap also reduces the new credit available to cover the current deficit. The local comparison keeps this deposit exactly and bounds the released credit jointly with the reserve before the arrival. Both come from the same capped history; the bounds p~i​k≤αi​(k)≤αi\tilde{p}_{ik}\leq\alpha_{i}(k)\leq\alpha_{i} yield a lower bound on the reserve in terms of the released credit. A larger reserve makes α~i\widetilde{\alpha}_{i} smaller, reducing its quadratic charge for a given increase.

Section D.2 derives this relation and verifies the resulting numerical comparison. ∎

Declaration of AI Usage

The authors developed this work with the help of extensive back-and-forth interactions with GPT Astra. The concept of OCEC generators and a framework for constructing them from Poisson arrivals was proposed by the authors, who then guided the model’s exploration of mapping Poisson arrivals to exponential clocks, potential functions, and proof strategies. The authors selected and refined the suggested approaches to optimize the presentation of results in the paper. The model also assisted with the formulation of finite optimization problems, the implementation and debugging of numerical verification programs, and the organization and polishing of the manuscript. The authors verified the correctness of the results and take full responsibility for the algorithms, proofs, numerical certificates, and all other content of the paper.

B.4 Proof of Lemma 11 and Lemma 16

It suffices to prove Lemma 16. Let ν\nu be obtained from π\pi by a finite sequence of matching and gap updates, and let xjx_{j} denote the mass of matching request jj. Realize the ages by a stationary rate-λ\lambda Poisson process on (−∞,t](-\infty,t], where tt is the total length of all updates and the matching requests and gaps occupy consecutive intervals of [0,t][0,t] in the order of the updates. Given the process, ii loses matching request jj independently with probability 1−Dxj​(bj)1-D_{x_{j}}(b_{j}), where bjb_{j} is its first age. No loss condition is imposed during gaps.

For r≤tr\leq t, let P⁡(r)P(r) denote the probability that ii loses every matching request after the arrivals in (r,t](r,t] are removed. An empty request interval remains empty. Since Dx​(b)≥Dx​(0)D_{x}(b)\geq D_{x}(0) by Lemma 29, removing more arrivals can only increase the probability of losing every matching request. Hence, PP is nonincreasing in rr.

The event A⁡(t)≥aA(t)\geq a means no arrival in (t−a,t](t-a,t]. It has probability e−λ​ae^{-\lambda a} and, by independent increments, conditioning on it does not affect the process before t−at-a. The stated tail bounds follow from its value ν​𝟏\nu\mathbf{1} at a=0a=0. ∎

C.2 Reachability and Monotonicity

34Tail restrictions.

For every reachable state, ν0,ν1\nu_{0},\nu_{1} are absolutely continuous and, with σ=ν0+2​ν1\sigma=\nu_{0}+2\nu_{1}, both functions a↦eλ​a​η​([a,∞))a\mapsto e^{\lambda a}\eta([a,\infty)), η∈{ν0,σ}\eta\in\{\nu_{0},\sigma\}, are nondecreasing with values in [0,1][0,1].

Proof.

Fix the requests (b¯j,xj)(\bar{b}_{j},x_{j}) with large bids so far, omitting zero masses, and put t=∑jxjt=\sum_{j}x_{j}. Realize the stationary age process by a rate-λ\lambda Poisson process on the real line. Conditional on this path, request jj is won with probability Dxj​(A^j)D_{x_{j}}(\widehat{A}_{j}) from (30), independently across requests; a request of mass one is won surely. For r∈[0,t]r\in[0,t], suppress arrivals after rr, retaining each request’s full mass, and use the same comparison uniforms. Let S⁡(r)S(r) be the resulting set of wins. Increasing rr changes a request’s first age from zero to its original positive value when its first arrival is restored. Since Dx​(a)≥Dx​(0)D_{x}(a)\geq D_{x}(0) for a>0a>0, the sets S⁡(r)S(r) increase.

The weights defining the two measures are

q0(S)=𝟏{S=∅},qσ(S)={1,S=∅,2​(1−b¯j),S={j},0,|S|≥2.q_{0}(S)=\mathbf{1}\{S=\varnothing\},\qquad q_{\sigma}(S)=\begin{cases}1,&S=\varnothing,\\ 2(1-\bar{b}_{j}),&S=\{j\},\\ 0,&|S|\geq 2.\end{cases}

Both lie in [0,1][0,1] and decrease when wins are added, since b¯j≥1/2\bar{b}_{j}\geq 1/2. Thus Vη​(r):=𝐄⁡[qη​(S⁡(r))]V_{\eta}(r):=\mathbf{E}[q_{\eta}(S(r))] is nonincreasing. Conditioning on no arrival in (t−a,t](t-a,t] and using independence of Poisson increments gives

η⁡([a,∞))=e−λ​a​Vη​((t−a)+).\eta([a,\infty))=e^{-\lambda a}V_{\eta}((t-a)_{+}).

For a>ta>t, all requests are empty and their comparison probabilities are independent of the initial age, giving the same formula with Vη​(0)V_{\eta}(0). This proves the tail claim. The weights are at most one, so ν0,σ≤π\nu_{0},\sigma\leq\pi as measures; hence both, and also ν1\nu_{1}, are absolutely continuous. Requests with small bids leave these measures fixed. ∎

Coefficient conditions.

The shape constraints in (49) make GsG_{s} and Fs−Gs/2F_{s}-G_{s}/2 nonnegative and nonincreasing in zz. Indeed, nonnegative Bernstein coefficients imply nonnegativity, while p′​(z)=d​∑j=0d−1(pj+1−pj)​ℬjd−1​(z)p^{\prime}(z)=d\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}(p_{j+1}-p_{j})\mathcal{B}_{j}^{d-1}(z) shows that nonincreasing coefficients imply p′≤0p^{\prime}\leq 0. ∂sFs≤2​Fs,∂sGs≤2​Gs,\partial_{s}F_{s}\leq 2F_{s},\qquad\partial_{s}G_{s}\leq 2G_{s}, (51)

so both prices are nonincreasing in ss. Checks at the two endpoints of each load interval suffice, using its one-sided derivative. Fix a reachable incoming state and normalized bid b¯\bar{b}. Let ff be bounded, continuous, nonnegative, and nondecreasing in age.
